q.q: Demand is Q=120−3P. Compare P=$30 with P=$10. Which statement explains why a constant slope does not imply constant point elasticity?
options: Both points have |Ed|=3 because the demand slope is −3, so revenue falls at both.
At $30, Q=30 and |Ed|=3; at $10, Q=90 and |Ed|=1/3, so a small price rise lowers revenue at the first point but raises it at the second.
At $30, |Ed|=1/3; at $10, |Ed|=3, so revenue effects are reversed.
Both points have unit elasticity because the demand equation is linear.
q.feedback: Point elasticity is |dQ/dP|×P/Q. It equals 3×30/30=3 at the high price and 3×10/90=1/3 at the low price. The P/Q ratio changes even though slope does not.

key: At $30, Q=30 and |Ed|=3; at $10, Q=90 and |Ed|=1/3, so a small price rise lowers revenue at the first point but raises it at the second.

q.q: Supply is Q=20+2P. At P=$20, a planner uses the slope 2 as elasticity and forecasts a 20% quantity rise after a small 10% price increase. Which correction is correct?
options: Elasticity is 2 because slope and elasticity are equal for any straight line; the 20% forecast is correct.
Elasticity is 60/20=3; the quantity response is approximately 30%.
Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.
Elasticity is 0.67, so quantity falls 6.7% when price rises.
q.feedback: At P=20, Q=60. Elasticity multiplies slope by P/Q: 2×20/60=2/3. The forecast quantity response is (2/3)×10%≈6.7%.

key: Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.

q.q: A rival’s 10% price cut reduces a firm’s sales by 15%, with its own price held fixed. Using the resulting cross-price elasticity, what would a small 4% rival price increase predict, and what relationship is indicated?
options: About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.
About a 6% sales decline; the goods are complements because the original sales change was negative.
About a 1.5% sales increase; elasticity is already a percentage forecast.
About a 2.7% sales increase; use the reciprocal of the observed response ratio.
q.feedback: The ratio is (−15%)/(−10%)=+1.5. A 4% rival-price rise predicts 1.5×4%=6% more sales, consistent with substitution.

key: About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.

q.q: Income falls 4% and product demand rises 6%, with prices and other determinants unchanged. If the estimated income elasticity applies to a subsequent small 2% income increase, what is the forecast and classification?
options: Demand rises about 3%; discard the negative sign when using income elasticity.
Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.
Demand falls about 1.5%; the elasticity coefficient itself is the forecast percentage.
Demand rises about 8%; add the observed quantity change to the new income change.
q.feedback: Income elasticity is 6/(−4)=−1.5. Multiplying by the new +2% income change gives −3%. Its negative sign identifies an inferior good over this range.

key: Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.

q.q: A wage floor raises the wage employers pay by 10%. Estimated labor-demand elasticity is −1.4 in the short run and −2 in the long run. A forecast says employment must fall exactly 14% in both periods. Which correction follows under the stated fixed-demand-determinant estimates?
options: The approximate declines are 1.4% and 2%; elasticity coefficients already state total percentage changes.
Employment rises 14% and 20% because labor supply slopes upward.
Employment falls 14% in both periods because the same wage change implies the same quantity response.
The approximate declines are 14% and 20%; longer-run substitution makes the second response larger.
q.feedback: Multiply each elasticity by +10%: −14% and −20%. These are local approximations, not exact universal predictions, and different horizons need not share one elasticity.

key: The approximate declines are 14% and 20%; longer-run substitution makes the second response larger.

q.q: Use the two labeled points on vertical D2. A student correctly computes zero midpoint demand elasticity, then concludes that total revenue is unchanged between the points. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Zero quantity change gives zero elasticity, but the higher-price point has higher revenue because the same positive quantity sells at a higher price.
Zero elasticity also means zero price change, so equal revenue follows.
Zero elasticity means quantity rises enough to offset the price rise, so equal revenue follows.
A vertical demand curve has infinite elasticity, so the midpoint calculation must be reversed.
q.feedback: For vertical D2, quantity is unchanged while price differs. The midpoint quantity-change numerator is zero. Revenue is P×Q, so with a positive fixed Q the higher price produces higher revenue.

key: Zero quantity change gives zero elasticity, but the higher-price point has higher revenue because the same positive quantity sells at a higher price.

q.q: A price-comparison service makes close substitutes easier to find. Before its launch a 5% price increase reduced sales by 2%; afterwards the same increase reduces sales by 8%, over equal adjustment periods. Which interpretation and revenue prediction fit the evidence?
options: Absolute demand elasticity falls from 2.5 to 0.625; a small price increase now tends to raise revenue.
Demand becomes more elastic solely because the firm moves upward along an unchanged demand curve; comparison information plays no role.
Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.
Demand remains inelastic because both tests use the same price increase; quantity responses cannot change the classification.
q.feedback: The response ratios are 2/5=0.4 and 8/5=1.6. Easier comparison improves substitution options. Above unit elasticity, the percentage quantity loss outweighs a small price increase.

key: Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.

q.q: A seller forecasts that a 5% price rise will raise revenue using today’s demand elasticity of 0.4. A close substitute launches before the planned price rise. Which revision and test would make the forecast more defensible?
options: Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.
Keep 0.4 because elasticity is a permanent property of the product; test only whether accounting costs changed.
Raise the revenue forecast automatically because a new substitute always increases demand for this seller’s product.
Use supply elasticity in place of demand elasticity because another producer has entered.
q.feedback: The new substitute changes buyers’ alternatives. The revenue prediction depends on responsiveness at the time of the price change, so an estimate above one can overturn the old inelastic-demand forecast.

key: Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.

q.q: Two customer groups buy the same product at the same price. A 4% price increase reduces Group A’s purchases by 2% and Group B’s by 8%. Both groups have the same adjustment period. B spends a larger income share on the product and has more substitutes. Which conclusion is justified?
options: A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.
A is more responsive than B because a smaller quantity response gives the larger elasticity.
Both have the same elasticity because price and adjustment period are the same; the responses measure supply instead.
The comparison proves that time horizon explains the difference, despite the identical adjustment periods.
q.feedback: The absolute elasticities are 0.5 and 2. Greater budget exposure and more substitutes are plausible reasons for B’s stronger response; the equal time horizon rules out that particular explanation.

key: A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.

q.q: A seller sees no quantity response after a tiny price test. Why is concluding perfectly inelastic demand premature?
options: The zero response estimates elasticity precisely at zero; repeat the same tiny test only to check the seller’s revenue arithmetic.
The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.
The test establishes elastic demand because buyers delayed purchases; a larger increase must therefore raise revenue.
The test establishes unit elasticity because quantity was stable; the next test should hold total revenue constant.
q.feedback: Observed response may be imprecise or constrained over the test window.

key: The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.

q.q: A national housing-supply estimate is 1.2 over ten years. City A has little buildable land and a one-year planning horizon; City B has available land and a ten-year horizon. Which use of the estimate is defensible?
options: Apply 1.2 to both cities because a national elasticity incorporates each local constraint equally.
Apply a larger elasticity to A because scarce land makes each price increase more valuable to owners.
Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.
Apply zero elasticity to B because a longer horizon fixes the housing stock more tightly.
q.feedback: Supply responsiveness depends on available resources and adjustment time. A national long-horizon estimate cannot identify either city’s elasticity without local evidence, particularly A’s constrained short-run response.

key: Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.

q.q: A firm estimates the price elasticity of demand at 1.05, with a wide confidence interval spanning values below and above one. What is the prudent pricing conclusion?
options: The price increase should lower revenue because the point estimate exceeds one; the interval affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
The price increase should raise revenue because the interval includes inelastic values; the point estimate affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
Revenue should be unchanged because the interval includes one; averaging elastic and inelastic estimates guarantees unit elasticity.
The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.
q.feedback: Sampling uncertainty around one makes the revenue prediction ambiguous.

key: The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.

q.q: A product is a necessity but has many close generic substitutes. Which determinant should dominate brand-level demand?
options: Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.
Brand demand should be less elastic than category demand, because a brand includes fewer possible purchases than the category.
Brand and category demand should have equal elasticity, because both purchases satisfy the same basic need.
Brand demand can be elastic only if the entire category is a luxury, because generic substitutes cannot change necessity status.
q.feedback: Elasticity depends on the defined choice set.

key: Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.

q.q: A product has no close substitutes today but represents a large budget share. What is the best conclusion?
options: Few substitutes establish inelastic demand; budget share changes spending levels but cannot affect responsiveness.
Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
The large budget share establishes elastic demand; the absence of substitutes changes price but cannot affect responsiveness.
The two determinants imply unit elasticity; their opposing directions necessarily cancel quantitatively.
q.feedback: Elasticity determinants are tendencies, not mechanical rules.

key: Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.

q.q: A market’s supply is inelastic today but highly elastic over five years. A permanent tax is imposed. How should incidence analysis change over time?
options: If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to sellers.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, supply adjustment raises the quantity traded but leaves the burden shares at their short-run values.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, producers’ ability to adjust makes the statutory taxpayer bear a larger share over time.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to buyers.
q.feedback: Relative elasticities evolve as producers gain exit and adjustment options.

key: If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to buyers.

q.q: A crop quota reduces sales from 1,000 to 900 units and raises price from $10 to $12. Farmers’ variable production cost falls by $300, while administering the quota uses $1,200 of their resources. Which comparison avoids confusing revenue with profit?
options: Revenue rises by $800 and profit must rise by $800 because the demand response is inelastic.
Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
Revenue falls by $1,000 and profit falls by $1,900 because fewer units are sold.
Revenue rises by $1,200 and profit rises by $300 because use the old quantity at the new price.
q.feedback: Revenue changes from $10,000 to $10,800. Profit changes by +800+300−1,200=−$100. Inelastic response can raise revenue without making an administratively costly policy profitable.

key: Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.

q.q: A seller estimates elastic demand but still raises price after a cost increase. Why is this not necessarily irrational?
options: Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, so profit must fall by the same amount even if the firm avoids variable costs.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue gain from a price rise, and that gain is sufficient to establish a profit gain after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, but reduced unit sales and higher contribution margins may improve profit after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts unchanged revenue from a price rise, so the cost increase can be passed on without checking the quantity response.
q.feedback: Revenue and profit are different objectives; cost pass-through depends on the full optimization problem.

key: Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, but reduced unit sales and higher contribution margins may improve profit after the cost increase.

q.q: A seller expects a small discount to increase revenue from customers with elastic demand. Those customers can freely resell purchases to customers currently paying the regular price. Which issue must the forecast address before treating the two groups’ sales as separate?
options: Resale guarantees the discount raises profit because every discounted sale is an additional market sale.
Resale makes both groups’ demand perfectly inelastic because the seller names two prices.
Resale affects fixed cost only, so it can be ignored when estimating demand responses.
Resale can shift regular-price purchases into the discounted channel; evaluate that switching as well as each group’s quantity response.
q.feedback: The elastic group may buy partly for resale, replacing rather than adding to regular-price sales. Separate response estimates do not by themselves establish the seller’s overall revenue or profit gain.

key: Resale can shift regular-price purchases into the discounted channel; evaluate that switching as well as each group’s quantity response.

q.q: An importer initially cuts foreign-goods purchases by 2% when their domestic-currency price rises 5%. After close domestic substitutes appear, the same price increase cuts imports 9%. If foreign prices and currency needed per imported unit are unchanged, which implication follows?
options: Import demand becomes more elastic, so the derived quantity demand for foreign currency becomes more responsive to the same domestic-currency price change.
Import demand becomes less elastic because 9% is larger than 2%, so foreign-currency purchases become less responsive.
The foreign-currency quantity must rise when imports fall, because each imported unit now requires more foreign currency.
Derived demand is unchanged because domestic substitutes cannot affect purchases of foreign goods.
q.feedback: The import response ratio rises from 0.4 to 1.8. With unchanged foreign currency required per unit, a larger percentage fall in imports produces a larger fall in currency purchases.

key: Import demand becomes more elastic, so the derived quantity demand for foreign currency becomes more responsive to the same domestic-currency price change.

q.q: A rival cuts its price 10%. Your product’s cross-price elasticity with that rival is +1.5, while your own-price elasticity is −0.5. Holding your price and other determinants fixed, which forecast and interpretation fit?
options: Your sales rise about 15%; positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are complements.
Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
Your sales rise about 5%; use own-price elasticity with the rival’s price cut.
Your sales fall about 0.15%; multiply by the elasticity as though it were already a percentage.
q.feedback: Use the cross-price coefficient for a rival’s price: 1.5×(−10%)=−15%. The positive relationship between rival price and own sales is the substitute pattern.

key: Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.

q.q: Income is forecast to rise 5%. Transit demand has income elasticity −0.6; leisure-rail demand has income elasticity +1.4. Prices and other determinants are fixed. Which forecast separates the sign from responsiveness?
options: Transit demand rises about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; discard the minus sign before forecasting.
Transit demand falls about 0.6%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 1.4%; coefficients are percentage changes themselves.
Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
Both demands rise 5% because the income shock is common to the two markets.
q.feedback: Multiply each coefficient by the 5% income rise: −0.6×5%=−3% and 1.4×5%=7%. For income elasticity, the sign identifies the direction and must be retained.

key: Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.

q.q: A producer’s price rises 8%. Its short-run supply elasticity is 0.25 and its long-run elasticity is 1.5, each applicable near the initial price. Which forecast and explanation fit, with other determinants held constant?
options: Quantity supplied rises 12% in the short run and 2% in the long run because time reduces adjustment options.
Quantity supplied rises 8% in both periods because elasticity measures the direction but not the size of the response.
Quantity supplied falls 2% then 12% because the higher output price raises the firm’s input costs by definition.
Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.
q.feedback: Supply response is elasticity times the price change: 0.25×8%=2% and 1.5×8%=12%. Longer adjustment time can allow greater output response.

key: Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.

q.q: Two reports describe the same demand estimate as −2.3 and 2.3. A manager says they predict opposite sales responses to a 2% price increase. Which diagnosis is appropriate if the second report uses the absolute-value convention?
options: Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.
One predicts a 4.6% decline and the other a 4.6% rise because absolute values reverse economic behavior.
Both predict a 2.3% sales decline because elasticity should not be multiplied by the price change.
Neither permits a revenue prediction because opposite printed signs prove the data disagree.
q.feedback: The signed estimate gives −2.3×2%=−4.6%. Reporting |Ed|=2.3 retains that downward-demand interpretation; it changes notation, not the estimated behavior.

key: Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.

q.q: A product has cross-price elasticity −0.9 with a companion service. The service price falls 10%. An analyst discards the minus sign and forecasts a 9% product-sales decline. Which correction is right?
options: Discard the sign: product sales fall about 9%, consistent with the purchases being substitutes.
Keep the sign: product sales fall about 0.9%, because the coefficient already contains the 10% price change.
Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.
Discard both signs: product sales are unchanged because cross-price elasticity cannot predict quantity.
q.feedback: For cross-price elasticity the sign distinguishes complements from substitutes. (−0.9)×(−10%)=+9%, so a cheaper complement raises demand for the product.

key: Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.

q.q: A binding posted-price ceiling holds the seller’s receipt at $10. Buyers must also pay a $2 per-unit tax, and approved buyers receive a $1 per-unit subsidy. Supply at the ceiling is only 60 units while buyers seek 100. Which analysis correctly distinguishes prices from actual trades?
options: Approved buyers pay $9 and sellers receive $12; all 100 desired units trade because the subsidy removes scarcity.
Approved buyers pay $13 and sellers receive $10; trades are 100 because all policy amounts should be added to demand.
Approved buyers pay $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are necessarily 100 because those prices clear any market.
Approved buyers’ net monetary outlay is $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are limited to 60, so a demand-elasticity calculation alone cannot establish 100 sales.
q.feedback: For approved buyers, $10+$2−$1=$11. Sellers still receive the capped $10, at which only 60 units are supplied. The binding shortage constrains actual trades regardless of desired purchases.

key: Approved buyers’ net monetary outlay is $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are limited to 60, so a demand-elasticity calculation alone cannot establish 100 sales.

q.q: A firm has customer-level elasticity estimates, capacity constraints, and rising marginal cost. Why is charging the lowest price to the most elastic customers not automatically optimal?
options: A lower price may attract more units from responsive customers, but those units use scarce capacity and may carry rising marginal cost; compare incremental contribution across feasible uses.
A lower price attracts more units from responsive customers, so allocate all capacity to them even when their incremental contribution is lower.
Rising marginal cost changes total profit but not the contribution of extra units, so allocate capacity using elasticity alone.
A capacity limit makes demand responses irrelevant until capacity expands, so allocate current capacity only by customers’ average spending.
q.feedback: Optimal pricing integrates demand response with costs and capacity.

key: A lower price may attract more units from responsive customers, but those units use scarce capacity and may carry rising marginal cost; compare incremental contribution across feasible uses.

q.q: Demand elasticity has magnitude 0.3 and supply elasticity is 1.2 in a competitive market. Which side bears more of a small per-unit tax?
options: Sellers, because supply is more elastic.
Both equally, because the tax is per unit.
Buyers, because demand is less elastic.
The side legally sending the payment, regardless of elasticity.
q.feedback: Buyers adjust quantity less readily than sellers; the less elastic side bears more of the tax.

key: Buyers, because demand is less elastic.

q.q: Two competitive markets receive the same $4 per-unit tax and have linear curves with no other distortions. Quantity falls by 10 units in A and 30 in B. Which has the greater deadweight loss?
options: A: $40 versus B: $120
Both: $4
B: $120 versus A: $40
B: $60 versus A: $20
q.feedback: DWL is half the tax wedge times lost quantity: A=0.5×4×10=$20 and B=0.5×4×30=$60.

key: B: $60 versus A: $20

q.q: Labor-demand elasticity is −0.8. With other conditions fixed, use the small-change approximation to predict employment after a 5% wage increase.
options: Employment rises about 4%.
Employment falls about 6.25%.
Employment rises about 5%.
Employment falls about 4%.
q.feedback: Percentage employment change is −0.8×5%=−4%; labor is the input demanded.

key: Employment falls about 4%.

q.q: A factory’s output imposes an unpriced $3 external cost per unit. A corrective tax raises its relevant per-unit cost, and output demand is price-responsive. Which outcome is consistent with the purpose of the tax?
options: Output falls as the firm faces more of the social cost of production.
Output rises because an external cost is an extra benefit.
The tax is justified only if output cannot change.
The external cost disappears solely because tax revenue is collected.
q.feedback: The unpriced harm motivates correction; incorporating that cost can reduce output and associated harm. Revenue collection itself is not removal of the physical externality.

key: Output falls as the firm faces more of the social cost of production.

q.q: A demand point has price $12 and quantity 50. What is total revenue at that point?
q.feedback: Multiply price by units sold: $12×50=$600.

q.q: A seller is on a smooth downward-sloping demand segment with |Ed|=2. Is selling a little more output associated with positive or negative marginal revenue?
options: Positive: the quantity gain outweighs the price reduction’s effect on revenue.
Negative: every price reduction lowers total revenue.
Zero: every point on demand maximizes revenue.
Negative: elastic demand means quantity barely responds.
q.feedback: On an elastic segment, a small price reduction raises total revenue, so the extra output has positive MR.

key: Positive: the quantity gain outweighs the price reduction’s effect on revenue.

q.q: A seller receives $18 per unit and sells 400 units after a change. What is its total revenue?
q.feedback: Total revenue is 18×400=$7,200, regardless of costs.

q.q: The graph’s competitive equilibrium is $20 per hour. A binding wage floor holds wages at $30, where labor supplied exceeds labor demanded. If the floor is removed with both curves unchanged, which adjustment is consistent with the model?
options: The wage falls toward $20; labor demand shifts right and labor supply shifts left solely because the wage falls.
The wage rises above $30; excess labor supply indicates employers cannot recruit enough workers.
The wage falls toward $20; labor demanded rises and labor supplied falls along their existing curves.
The wage stays at $30; removing the floor changes only the label attached to unemployment.
q.commonError: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
q.feedback: At the enforced above-equilibrium wage there is excess labor supply. Removing it permits a lower wage, increasing hiring and reducing the quantity offered along unchanged curves until they meet.
q.imageAlt: Warehouse labor demand and supply intersect at 4,000 workers and an hourly wage of $20.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars. The horizontal axis is hundreds of warehouse workers. Labor demand slopes downward and labor supply slopes upward. Their marked intersection is at 40 on the horizontal scale, or 4,000 workers, and $20 per hour.

key: The wage falls toward $20; labor demanded rises and labor supplied falls along their existing curves.

q.q: At 6,000 workers in the graph, the wage required by labor supply exceeds firms’ marginal willingness to pay on labor demand. A proposal forces hiring up to that level without changing productivity or workers’ opportunity costs. Which marginal assessment is correct?
options: Every extra wage dollar is a net social gain, so hiring beyond the demand-supply intersection must raise surplus.
Some additional hires have opportunity cost above their marginal product value; wage payments alone do not establish a net social gain.
Marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost because labor supply lies above demand at 6,000.
No marginal comparison is possible because labor demand measures average rather than marginal product value.
q.commonError: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
q.feedback: Labor supply reflects workers’ marginal opportunity cost and demand their marginal product value in this competitive model. When supply lies above demand, forcing those extra hires uses resources worth more than the output they add.
q.imageAlt: Warehouse labor demand and supply intersect at 4,000 workers and an hourly wage of $20.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars. The horizontal axis is hundreds of warehouse workers. Labor demand slopes downward and labor supply slopes upward. Their marked intersection is at 40 on the horizontal scale, or 4,000 workers, and $20 per hour.

key: Some additional hires have opportunity cost above their marginal product value; wage payments alone do not establish a net social gain.

q.q: The graph moves from 4,000 warehouse workers at $20 to 6,000 at $25 with labor supply unchanged. A manager attributes the increase to more workers becoming available at every wage. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The manager is correct because any rise in employment must be a rightward labor-supply shift.
The graph shows movement down unchanged labor demand because the wage rose.
The graph shows lower labor demand because higher wages reduce firms’ desired employment at every wage.
The graph instead shows greater labor demand; employment rises despite a higher wage, while a supply expansion alone would tend to lower the wage.
q.commonError: Reverses the wage or employment effect of a labor-demand shift.
q.feedback: The new outcome has both higher wage and employment and is on the unchanged supply curve. A rightward demand shift accounts for both; a supply expansion alone has a different wage direction.
q.imageAlt: Warehouse labor demand shifts right, raising equilibrium from 4,000 workers at $20 to 6,000 workers at $25 per hour.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of warehouse workers. Supply is unchanged. Labor demand shifts right from dashed D L0 to solid D L1. The marked equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 per hour to 6,000 workers at $25 per hour.

key: The graph instead shows greater labor demand; employment rises despite a higher wage, while a supply expansion alone would tend to lower the wage.

q.q: The graph shows warehouse labor demand increasing. Suppose a sorting system raises marginal product by 25% at every employment level, but the competitive output price simultaneously falls by 10%. How does value of marginal product compare with its original level, and does that support the depicted demand shift?
options: It rises by 15%, supporting a rightward shift because the percentage changes should simply be subtracted.
It falls by 10%, contradicting the shift because product price alone determines labor demand.
It rises by 12.5%, supporting a rightward demand shift because 1.25×0.90=1.125.
It remains unchanged because a productivity gain and a price decline always cancel.
q.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
q.feedback: VMP is product price times marginal product. Combining the two changes gives 1.25×0.90=1.125, a 12.5% increase at each employment level, supporting increased labor demand.
q.imageAlt: Warehouse labor demand shifts right, raising equilibrium from 4,000 workers at $20 to 6,000 workers at $25 per hour.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of warehouse workers. Supply is unchanged. Labor demand shifts right from dashed D L0 to solid D L1. The marked equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 per hour to 6,000 workers at $25 per hour.

key: It rises by 12.5%, supporting a rightward demand shift because 1.25×0.90=1.125.

q.q: The graph shows D L0 shifting to D L1 while labor supply stays fixed. A report says “the higher wage caused labor demand to increase.” Which sequence correctly separates cause from movement?
options: The higher wage shifts labor demand right; the extra employment then shifts labor supply left.
An increase in productivity or output demand raises labor demand; the resulting higher wage brings movement along unchanged labor supply.
The higher wage moves employers down their original demand curve; no demand shifter is required.
Labor supply shifts right first; the higher wage is the normal result of that supply expansion.
q.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
q.feedback: A wage change moves quantity demanded along a labor-demand curve; it does not shift that curve. A demand determinant changes first, and the new equilibrium includes movement along supply.
q.imageAlt: Warehouse labor demand shifts right, raising equilibrium from 4,000 workers at $20 to 6,000 workers at $25 per hour.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of warehouse workers. Supply is unchanged. Labor demand shifts right from dashed D L0 to solid D L1. The marked equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 per hour to 6,000 workers at $25 per hour.

key: An increase in productivity or output demand raises labor demand; the resulting higher wage brings movement along unchanged labor supply.

q.q: A disease reduces each orchard worker’s marginal product by 20%, but the fruit price rises by 25%. Assume competitive output pricing and the same percentage productivity effect at each employment level. Does the graph’s leftward labor-demand shift necessarily follow after both changes?
options: Yes; a productivity decline shifts labor demand left regardless of product price.
No; VMP rises by 5% because the percentage changes should be added algebraically.
Yes; the fruit-price rise lowers VMP by increasing workers’ opportunity cost.
No; VMP is unchanged because 0.80×1.25=1, so the productivity loss alone does not determine the combined labor-demand effect.
q.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
q.feedback: Derived demand depends on price times marginal product. The stated price rise exactly offsets the productivity decline: 1.25×0.80=1. Neither effect can be considered alone.
q.imageAlt: Orchard labor demand shifts left, lowering equilibrium from 4,000 workers at $20 to 2,000 workers at $15 per hour.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of orchard workers. Supply is unchanged. Labor demand shifts left from dashed D L0 to solid D L1. The marked equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 per hour to 2,000 workers at $15 per hour.

key: No; VMP is unchanged because 0.80×1.25=1, so the productivity loss alone does not determine the combined labor-demand effect.

q.q: The graph marks employment at 40 on an axis measured in hundreds, with wage $20. A later equilibrium is 60 on the same scale at wage $25. An analyst reports payroll rises from $800 to $1,500, a 50% increase. Which correction is complete?
options: Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, a 50% increase because only employment matters.
Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, an 87.5% increase; both the axis scale and the wage change matter.
Payroll rises from $800 to $1,500, an 87.5% increase because the axis scale does not affect dollar totals.
Payroll rises from $80,000 to $100,000, a 25% increase because the wage change alone determines payroll.
q.commonError: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
q.feedback: Employment is 4,000 then 6,000. Payrolls are 4,000×20=$80,000 and 6,000×25=$150,000. The gain is 70,000/80,000=87.5%, combining price and quantity changes.
q.imageAlt: Warehouse labor demand and supply intersect at 4,000 workers and an hourly wage of $20.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars. The horizontal axis is hundreds of warehouse workers. Labor demand slopes downward and labor supply slopes upward. Their marked intersection is at 40 on the horizontal scale, or 4,000 workers, and $20 per hour.

key: Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, an 87.5% increase; both the axis scale and the wage change matter.

q.q: The orchard graph shows employment falling from 4,000 to 2,000 after a productivity loss at unchanged output price. A later output-price increase raises marginal revenue product, but its size is not given. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: The first employment loss is 2,000; any later price rise necessarily restores exactly 4,000 workers.
The first employment loss is 2,000; the later price rise partly offsets the demand reduction, but the final employment level relative to 4,000 is not determined.
The first employment loss is 200; a higher output price shifts labor supply right rather than demand.
The first employment loss is 4,000; the later price rise cannot affect derived labor demand.
q.commonError: Reverses the wage or employment effect of a labor-demand shift.
q.feedback: Read the initial change with the hundreds-of-workers scale: 4,000−2,000=2,000. A higher output price raises product value per worker, opposing the original demand loss. Without the magnitude, restoration to or beyond the original level is uncertain.
q.imageAlt: Orchard labor demand shifts left, lowering equilibrium from 4,000 workers at $20 to 2,000 workers at $15 per hour.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of orchard workers. Supply is unchanged. Labor demand shifts left from dashed D L0 to solid D L1. The marked equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 per hour to 2,000 workers at $15 per hour.

key: The first employment loss is 2,000; the later price rise partly offsets the demand reduction, but the final employment level relative to 4,000 is not determined.

q.q: Expanded nursing programs shift labor supply right as shown, from 4,000 nurses at $20 to 6,000 at $15. Hospitals then experience an increase in demand for care. With the size of that second shift unknown, which final comparison with the original equilibrium is justified?
options: Employment is higher and the wage must remain below $20 because the supply shift occurred first.
Employment is higher, but the wage can be below, equal to or above $20 because the supply and demand shifts have opposing wage effects.
Employment is lower and the wage must exceed $20 because demand shifts always reduce hiring.
Employment returns to 4,000 and the wage returns to $20 because two rightward shifts cancel.
q.commonError: Treats the wage as a labor-supply shifter rather than a cause of movement along labor supply.
q.feedback: More qualified workers and greater derived labor demand both support higher employment. Supply expansion tends to lower wages while demand expansion tends to raise them, so their relative strengths determine the final wage.
q.imageAlt: Healthcare labor supply shifts right, moving equilibrium from 4,000 workers at $20 to 6,000 workers at $15 per hour.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of healthcare workers. Labor demand is unchanged. Labor supply shifts right from dashed S L0 to solid S L1. The marked equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 per hour to 6,000 workers at $15 per hour.

key: Employment is higher, but the wage can be below, equal to or above $20 because the supply and demand shifts have opposing wage effects.

q.q: The restaurant graph shows an unregulated equilibrium of 4,000 workers at $15. At a $20 wage floor, firms demand 2,000 workers and 6,000 seek work. A report calls all 4,000 excess job seekers “jobs lost.” Which correction is right?
options: Jobs fall by 4,000 and excess labor supplied is 2,000 because both compare demand with the original employment level.
Jobs fall by 2,000, while excess labor supplied is 4,000; the latter includes additional workers attracted by the higher wage.
Jobs rise by 2,000 because labor supplied rises from 4,000 to 6,000.
Jobs remain 4,000 because a legal wage changes pay but not hiring.
q.commonError: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
q.feedback: Employment falls from 4,000 to 2,000, a 2,000-job decline. Excess supply at the floor is 6,000−2,000=4,000; that differs from the fall in jobs.
q.imageAlt: A $20 minimum wage lies above the $15 competitive restaurant wage, with labor demanded of 2,000 and labor supplied of 6,000 workers.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of restaurant workers. Competitive labor demand and supply intersect at 4,000 workers and $15 per hour. A horizontal minimum wage at $20 intersects labor demand at 2,000 workers and labor supply at 6,000 workers, creating a labor surplus of 4,000 workers.
q.laborMarketScenario: binding minimum wage in a restaurant labor market

key: Jobs fall by 2,000, while excess labor supplied is 4,000; the latter includes additional workers attracted by the higher wage.

q.q: The monopsony graph shows hiring of 4,000 nurses at wage $20, where MFC=MRP=$30. The competitive intersection of supply and MRP is 6,000 at $25. Which comparison explains why expanding employment toward the competitive level can raise surplus despite a higher wage?
options: The higher wage is itself a resource benefit that proves every possible employment expansion raises surplus.
Between those levels, nurses’ opportunity cost on supply is below their marginal product value; the wage is a transfer, while monopsony restricts mutually beneficial employment.
MFC=$30 means all 4,000 nurses already receive $30, so the competitive outcome reduces their wage.
Supply above MRP between those levels means the extra nurses cost more than the output they add.
q.commonError: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
q.feedback: The employer uses MFC rather than the wage to choose hiring. At its restricted outcome, supply lies below MRP; the additional employment toward their intersection creates gains because marginal output value exceeds workers’ opportunity cost.
q.imageAlt: A nursing monopsony hires 4,000 nurses where MFC equals MRP and pays $20 on labor supply; competition would employ 6,000 at $25.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is hourly wage in dollars and the horizontal axis is hundreds of nurses. Labor supply slopes upward, marginal factor cost rises more steeply, and marginal revenue product slopes downward. MFC equals MRP at 4,000 nurses and $30 of marginal factor cost; the wage read from labor supply at that employment is $20. Labor supply intersects MRP at the competitive outcome of 6,000 nurses and $25 per hour.

key: Between those levels, nurses’ opportunity cost on supply is below their marginal product value; the wage is a transfer, while monopsony restricts mutually beneficial employment.

q.q: At a delivery firm, one worker adds 30 parcels and the next adds 22. The following worker would add 14. Each parcel sells for $6 and each additional worker costs $100, with other costs unchanged. Which hiring conclusion distinguishes diminishing marginal product from profitability?
options: Reject both workers because any decline in marginal product means extra output is unprofitable.
Hire the worker adding 22 parcels but not the one adding 14; their added revenues are $132 and $84 even though both have positive marginal product.
Hire both workers because positive marginal product is sufficient for profit to rise.
Hire only the worker adding 14 parcels because lower marginal product means lower marginal labor cost.
q.commonError: Confuses diminishing marginal product with falling total product or negative marginal product.
q.feedback: Compare added revenue with the $100 wage. 22×$6=$132 exceeds the wage; 14×$6=$84 does not. Diminishing marginal product need not mean negative marginal product or immediate unprofitability.

key: Hire the worker adding 22 parcels but not the one adding 14; their added revenues are $132 and $84 even though both have positive marginal product.

q.q: A program pays a landlord up to $500 for a recipient’s rent. The recipient cannot receive the amount as cash or spend it elsewhere. How is the benefit classified?
options: Unrestricted cash income
A wage premium for job risk
A loan owed by the recipient
An in-kind housing transfer
q.feedback: The restriction directs the benefit to housing rather than leaving its use to the recipient.

key: An in-kind housing transfer

q.q: Two otherwise identical jobs pay $24 and $28 per hour. The higher-paying job alone exposes workers to danger. What hourly premium is consistent with compensation for that danger?
q.feedback: The difference, $28 − $24 = $4 per hour, is the compensating premium, not the entire risky-job wage.

q.q: Two jobs have equal risk and amenities, but one requires scarce technical training. Why is a higher wage in that job not evidence of a compensating differential for danger?
options: Every wage difference is compensation for danger.
Training changes wealth but cannot affect earnings.
Equal danger implies equal productivity in both jobs.
The stated difference is skill scarcity, while risk is held equal.
q.feedback: A risk premium requires a difference in risk. Here skill requirements provide a distinct explanation of the wage gap.

key: The stated difference is skill scarcity, while risk is held equal.

q.q: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $31,000. A household has $31,000 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Poor because its income is below the threshold.
Poor because equality counts as below.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
Exactly at the threshold and not poor under this rule.
q.feedback: Compare 31000 with 31000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

key: Exactly at the threshold and not poor under this rule.

q.q: Policies A and B produce incomes (10, 80) and (15, 60) for two groups. Which does a maximin rule prefer?
options: A, because its total income is 90 rather than 75.
A, because its highest income is 80 rather than 60.
Neither, because maximin requires equal incomes.
B, because its lowest income is 15 rather than 10.
q.feedback: Maximin ranks the worst-off outcome: 15 exceeds 10 even though B has a smaller total.

key: B, because its lowest income is 15 rather than 10.

q.q: An evaluator accepts unequal holdings when they result from legitimate acquisition and voluntary exchange. Which additional fact would most directly challenge that evaluator’s acceptance?
options: The highest income is twice the lowest.
Part of the holdings resulted from theft.
A voluntary gift raises one person’s wealth.
The final distribution has a positive Gini coefficient.
q.feedback: Theft contradicts legitimate acquisition; inequality alone does not establish that contradiction under the stated criterion.

key: Part of the holdings resulted from theft.

q.q: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $30,000. A household has $28,400 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Above the threshold and not poor.
Exactly at the threshold.
Poor under this rule.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
q.feedback: Compare 28400 with 30000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

key: Poor under this rule.

q.q: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $26,000. A household has $25,000 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Above the threshold and not poor.
Exactly at the threshold.
Poor under this rule.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
q.feedback: Compare 25000 with 26000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

key: Poor under this rule.

q.q: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $30,000. A household has $31,800 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Poor because its income is below the threshold.
Exactly at the threshold.
Above the threshold and not poor under this rule.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
q.feedback: Compare 31800 with 30000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

key: Above the threshold and not poor under this rule.

q.q: A program withdraws a $600 benefit all at once when earnings cross a cutoff. A household earns $100 more and crosses that cutoff. With no other changes, what happens to disposable income?
options: It falls by $500.
It rises by $100.
It falls by $600.
It rises by $700.
q.feedback: The extra $100 is smaller than the $600 benefit loss: the net change is −$500.

key: It falls by $500.

q.q: A household earns $50 more and loses $30 of benefits, with no other changes. What is the implied benefit phaseout rate?
q.feedback: The benefit loss per extra earnings dollar is 30/50 = 0.60.

q.q: A safety improvement eliminates a job hazard without changing productivity, worker skills or other job amenities. In a competitive labor market, what happens to the compensating part of its wage?
options: It tends to rise because the job is safer.
It stays fixed because compensating differentials depend only on productivity.
It becomes an inheritance payment rather than labor income.
It tends to fall because the undesirable attribute has been removed.
q.feedback: Workers require less compensation for risk when the risk falls, holding other determinants of pay fixed.

key: It tends to fall because the undesirable attribute has been removed.

q.q: A household receives a one-time $60,000 inheritance and saves it. Its annual wage remains $30,000. Which statement correctly separates stocks and flows?
options: The inheritance raises its wage to $90,000 every year.
The inheritance raises its asset stock; it does not by itself raise its annual wage flow.
Saving the inheritance prevents it from affecting wealth.
The inheritance is a debt because it is not earned through labor.
q.feedback: Accumulated assets are wealth measured at a point in time. Wages are a flow over a period, and the inherited asset need not change that flow.

key: The inheritance raises its asset stock; it does not by itself raise its annual wage flow.

q.q: A household has $25,800 in measured income against a $27,000 poverty threshold. A cash grant counts dollar for dollar and changes no other income. What is the smallest grant that reaches the threshold?
q.feedback: The shortfall is $27,000 − $25,800 = $1,200. Reaching the threshold requires closing that gap.

q.q: A voluntary gift reduces wealth inequality, while a compulsory transfer would produce the same final distribution. Why might an entitlement-based evaluator distinguish them?
options: Identical final distributions necessarily imply identical acquisition processes.
Consent and legitimate acquisition affect the assessment even when final distributions match.
Voluntary gifts cannot change a wealth distribution.
An entitlement rule ranks arrangements solely by their Gini coefficients.
q.feedback: An entitlement view evaluates how holdings are obtained and transferred, so consent can matter independently of the final distribution.

key: Consent and legitimate acquisition affect the assessment even when final distributions match.

q.q: A benefit falls by $0.60 per additional dollar earned. With no taxes or other changes, how much does disposable income rise when earnings rise by $100?
q.feedback: The household gains $100 in earnings and loses $60 in benefits, leaving a $40 increase.

q.q: Two households each earn $50,000 from work. One inherits $100,000 and invests it at 4% per year; the other receives no inheritance. Ignoring taxes and other income, how do next year’s labor earnings and total incomes compare?
options: Labor earnings differ by $100,000; total income is equal.
Labor earnings are equal; the inheriting household has $4,000 more total income.
Labor earnings are equal; total income differs by $100,000 each year.
Both labor earnings and total income differ by $4,000.
q.feedback: An inheritance is an asset stock; its 4% return produces a $4,000 annual income flow without changing labor earnings.

key: Labor earnings are equal; the inheriting household has $4,000 more total income.

q.q: A recipient’s preferred bundle after a $100 cash grant contains only $40 of food. A $100 nonresalable food voucher replaces the grant at the same prices. What restriction matters?
options: The voucher allows all $100 to be spent on rent.
The voucher requires at least $100 of food purchases, excluding the preferred cash-grant bundle.
The voucher lowers every price by 60%.
The voucher expands the feasible set beyond that offered by cash.
q.feedback: The voucher is binding because desired food spending under cash is below $100; it cannot be exchanged for the preferred nonfood purchases.

key: The voucher requires at least $100 of food purchases, excluding the preferred cash-grant bundle.

q.q: A redistribution proposal raises the poorest group’s income from 10 to 14 and lowers total income from 100 to 94. One evaluator supports it; another rejects it solely because the total falls. What explains the disagreement?
options: They disagree about whether 14 exceeds 10.
The proposal is mathematically impossible.
They both apply maximin but calculate the same minimum differently.
They apply different normative criteria: the minimum versus total income.
q.feedback: The stated facts allow improved minimum income alongside a smaller total. The disagreement concerns what to value, not the arithmetic.

key: They apply different normative criteria: the minimum versus total income.

q.q: A household holds assets of $180,000 and debt of $70,000, including an inherited asset worth $40,000 already included in total assets. What is its net wealth?
q.feedback: Net wealth equals assets minus debt: $180,000 − $70,000 = $110,000. Adding the inheritance again would double-count it.

q.q: A recipient would spend $200 on food with a $100 cash grant. Instead the program offers a nonresalable $100 food voucher, with identical prices and no transaction costs. What can be inferred?
options: The voucher must reduce welfare because every spending restriction binds.
The voucher raises cash purchasing power by $200.
The voucher forces food spending to fall below $100.
The cash-optimal bundle remains feasible, so the restriction need not reduce this recipient’s welfare.
q.feedback: The intended food spending exceeds the voucher amount. The voucher can replace $100 of spending the recipient would already make, leaving the cash-optimal bundle feasible.

key: The cash-optimal bundle remains feasible, so the restriction need not reduce this recipient’s welfare.

q.q: Policy A yields group incomes (12, 100); B yields (18, 70). A third policy C yields (18, 90). Under a rule that first maximizes the minimum and breaks ties by total income, which policy is selected?
options: A
B
All three tie
C
q.feedback: B and C share the highest minimum, 18. The stated tie-break then selects C, whose total is 108 rather than 88.

key: C

q.q: A benefit phaseout takes $0.60 per extra earnings dollar and an earnings tax takes $0.20, both calculated independently on gross earnings. Reducing the phaseout to $0.30 leaves the tax unchanged. What happens to the net return from an extra $100 earned?
options: It rises from $40 to $70.
It falls from $80 to $50.
It rises from $20 to $50.
It stays at $20.
q.feedback: Initially the household keeps 100 − 60 − 20 = $20; afterward it keeps 100 − 30 − 20 = $50.

key: It rises from $20 to $50.

q.q: Two households have equal labor earnings. Household A inherits productive assets, while B does not. A proposal equalizes their current labor earnings but leaves asset ownership and returns unchanged. Which evaluation is justified?
options: The proposal eliminates the wealth gap because equal annual earnings imply equal asset stocks.
The proposal leaves this wealth gap and associated capital-income gap in place; equal labor earnings do not establish equal economic resources.
The proposal removes capital income by holding labor earnings equal.
The proposal increases labor productivity in B by transferring ownership of A’s assets.
q.feedback: A stock of inherited assets can persist and yield income independently of equal labor earnings. A labor-income rule alone does not transfer that stock.

key: The proposal leaves this wealth gap and associated capital-income gap in place; equal labor earnings do not establish equal economic resources.

q.q: A hypothetical poverty measure counts cash income but excludes food vouchers. A household has $25,000 in cash and $3,000 in vouchers; its threshold is $27,000. Replacing the vouchers with $3,000 cash changes no prices. Which conclusion follows?
options: Measured status remains below because transfers never enter cash income.
Measured status changes from above to below because vouchers are counted twice.
Measured status remains above because the original vouchers already count as cash.
Measured status changes from below to above the threshold, though this alone does not measure the change in well-being.
q.feedback: The measure initially counts $25,000 and then $28,000. Classification changes mechanically; the economic value of relaxing spending restrictions is a separate question.

key: Measured status changes from below to above the threshold, though this alone does not measure the change in well-being.

q.q: Two households each have $31,000 measured income. The threshold is $30,000 for the smaller household and $34,000 for the larger. An analyst classifies both as above poverty because their incomes match. What is the error?
options: The analyst should classify both below poverty because their incomes match.
The analyst should compare the smaller household with the larger household’s threshold only.
The analyst should average the thresholds before classifying either household.
The analyst ignores different applicable thresholds; only the smaller household is above its threshold.
q.feedback: Each household must be compared with its own specified threshold. Equal measured income need not imply equal classification.

key: The analyst ignores different applicable thresholds; only the smaller household is above its threshold.

q.q: One policy restores property proven to have been stolen; another redistributes legitimately acquired property to equalize incomes. Both lower inequality. What follows under an entitlement framework?
options: Both must be rejected because an entitlement framework prohibits any change in ownership.
The first may rectify a rights violation; the common distributional result does not make the two policies equivalent.
Both must be accepted because lower inequality is the sole entitlement criterion.
Neither can be assessed without knowing whether aggregate income rises.
q.feedback: Rectification of unjust acquisition differs from compulsory equalization of legitimate holdings. A shared effect on inequality does not erase that distinction.

key: The first may rectify a rights violation; the common distributional result does not make the two policies equivalent.

q.q: A program replaces a $1,000 benefit cliff at one earnings cutoff with a $0.20 reduction per dollar over the next $5,000. Which assessment is correct?
options: The abrupt $1,000 loss disappears, but the 20% phaseout weakens the marginal return to earnings across a wider range.
All work disincentives disappear because there is no longer a cliff.
The phaseout removes the benefit after only $200 of additional earnings.
Recipients throughout the phaseout keep every additional earnings dollar.
q.feedback: Spreading $1,000 over $5,000 produces a 20% phaseout. It smooths the discontinuity while applying a marginal benefit loss over the range.

key: The abrupt $1,000 loss disappears, but the 20% phaseout weakens the marginal return to earnings across a wider range.

q.q: A dangerous job pays more than a safe job, but its workers also have more training. After training is controlled for, the wage gap shrinks but remains positive. What does this evidence support?
options: Training explains the entire gap; the remaining difference is evidence against risk compensation.
Risk compensation explains the entire gap; the training adjustment is irrelevant.
The remaining gap measures inherited wealth rather than labor income.
Training explains part of the gap; the remainder is consistent with risk compensation but is not uniquely identified as such.
q.feedback: The observed gap mixes worker characteristics and job attributes. Controlling for training removes one competing explanation but does not establish that no other differences remain.

key: Training explains part of the gap; the remainder is consistent with risk compensation but is not uniquely identified as such.

q.q: An equal-cost cash grant gives recipients more choice than a restricted tutoring benefit. Suppose tutoring produces an external benefit not reflected in recipients’ choices. Which assessment is justified?
options: The external benefit makes the restricted benefit privately preferred by every recipient.
Cash weakly expands private choice; the external benefit gives a separate reason a policymaker might favor tutoring.
Greater private choice proves cash creates more total social benefit in every case.
Equal fiscal cost makes the restriction and the external benefit irrelevant.
q.feedback: Private choice and social spillovers are distinct criteria. An external benefit can motivate targeting even when recipients would choose another use for cash.

key: Cash weakly expands private choice; the external benefit gives a separate reason a policymaker might favor tutoring.

q.q: Use the Lorenz curve. If total income is $200 million, how much goes to the bottom 60%, and why would assigning them $120 million misread the graph?
options: $120 million; the equality line gives the observed income distribution.
$140 million; subtract their 30% income share from 100%.
$60 million; 60% is their population share, while their income share is 30%.
$30 million; treat the percentage income share as a dollar amount.
q.feedback: The curve assigns 30% of income to the bottom 60% of people. 0.30×$200 million=$60 million; equal population shares do not imply equal income shares.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curve showing the bottom 40 percent receiving 15 percent of income.
q.graphDescription: The equality line is diagonal. The Lorenz curve passes through cumulative population-income points (20,5), (40,15), (60,30), (80,55), and (100,100); the bottom-40-percent reading is highlighted.
q.graphScenario: single Lorenz curve with quintile readings

key: $60 million; 60% is their population share, while their income share is 30%.

q.q: The Lorenz curve gives the bottom 40% of households 15% of income. An analyst says this means their average income is 15% of the economy-wide mean. Which correction is right?
options: Their mean is 15% of the overall mean: use the cumulative income share alone.
Their mean is 37.5% of the overall mean: divide the income share by the population share.
Their mean is 40% of the overall mean: use the cumulative population share alone.
Their mean is 60% of the overall mean: use the population share outside this group.
q.feedback: The group receives 0.15 of income across 0.40 of households, so its average relative to the overall mean is 0.15/0.40=0.375.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curve showing the bottom 40 percent receiving 15 percent of income.
q.graphDescription: The equality line is diagonal. The Lorenz curve passes through cumulative population-income points (20,5), (40,15), (60,30), (80,55), and (100,100); the bottom-40-percent reading is highlighted.
q.graphScenario: single Lorenz curve with quintile readings

key: Their mean is 37.5% of the overall mean: divide the income share by the population share.

q.q: The graph assigns the bottom 40% a 22% income share in A and 7% in B. A has total income $100 million and B has $400 million. Which comparison distinguishes relative distribution from group income?
options: A has both the larger share and larger group income because 22% exceeds 7%.
B has the larger bottom-40% share because its total income is four times A’s.
The group receives equal income in A and B because each contains 40% of its population.
A has the larger bottom-40% share, but that group receives $22 million in A versus $28 million in B.
q.feedback: A’s group receives 0.22×100=$22 million; B’s receives 0.07×400=$28 million. Relative shares and absolute income totals answer different questions.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curves A and B, with B farther from equality than A.
q.graphDescription: Curve A passes through (20,10), (40,22), (60,40), and (80,65). Curve B passes through (20,2), (40,7), (60,17), and (80,40). B is farther below the equality line, and bottom-40-percent shares of 22 percent for A and 7 percent for B are highlighted.

key: A has the larger bottom-40% share, but that group receives $22 million in A versus $28 million in B.

q.q: Under curve B, the bottom 80% receive approximately 40% of income. A student assigns the remaining 60% to the top 40% of households. What is the correct group and average-income comparison?
options: It is the top 40%; its mean income is about 1.5 times the overall mean.
It is the top 20%; its mean income is about 0.6 times the overall mean.
It is the top 20%; its mean income is about three times the overall mean.
It is the bottom 20%; its mean income is about three times the overall mean.
q.feedback: The complement of the bottom 80% is the top 20%. It receives 60% of income, so its mean relative to the overall mean is 0.60/0.20=3.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curves A and B, with B farther from equality than A.
q.graphDescription: Curve A passes through (20,10), (40,22), (60,40), and (80,65). Curve B passes through (20,2), (40,7), (60,17), and (80,40). B is farther below the equality line, and bottom-40-percent shares of 22 percent for A and 7 percent for B are highlighted.

key: It is the top 20%; its mean income is about three times the overall mean.

q.q: Under curve A, cumulative income shares are approximately 22% at population 40% and 40% at population 60%. An analyst claims the intervening quintile has average income twice the economy-wide mean. Which correction fits the readings?
options: The quintile receives 40% of income, so its mean is twice the overall mean.
The quintile receives 18% of income, so its mean is about 90% of the overall mean.
The quintile receives 22% of income, so its mean is 110% of the overall mean.
The quintile receives 62% of income, so its mean is 310% of the overall mean.
q.feedback: The noncumulative share is 40−22=18%. Spread over 20% of households, this is 18/20=90% of the overall mean.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curves A and B, with B farther from equality than A.
q.graphDescription: Curve A passes through (20,10), (40,22), (60,40), and (80,65). Curve B passes through (20,2), (40,7), (60,17), and (80,40). B is farther below the equality line, and bottom-40-percent shares of 22 percent for A and 7 percent for B are highlighted.

key: The quintile receives 18% of income, so its mean is about 90% of the overall mean.

q.q: In the graph, the Gini falls and the Lorenz curve moves toward equality. Could a uniform 10% reduction in every household’s income, with nothing else changing, generate that distributional change?
options: Yes; a uniform proportional reduction necessarily moves the Lorenz curve toward equality.
Yes; a uniform proportional reduction eliminates the income gaps measured in percentages.
No; a uniform proportional reduction raises the Gini even though relative shares do not change.
No; a uniform proportional reduction lowers mean income but leaves relative income shares and the Gini unchanged.
q.feedback: Multiplying every income by 0.9 multiplies each group’s income and the total by the same factor. Shares and relative inequality do not change, so the displayed Gini decline requires a distributional change.
q.imageAlt: An after-policy Lorenz curve lies closer to equality than the before-policy curve; Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252.
q.graphDescription: Before-policy cumulative income shares are 5, 15, 30, and 55 percent at cumulative populations 20, 40, 60, and 80 percent. After-policy shares are 10, 22, 40, and 65 percent. The stated Gini coefficients are 0.380 before and 0.252 after.
q.graphScenario: before-and-after Lorenz curves with Gini values

key: No; a uniform proportional reduction lowers mean income but leaves relative income shares and the Gini unchanged.

q.q: The graph initially gives the lowest quintile 5% of income and the highest quintile 45%. Total income is initially $100 million. Later total income rises to $120 million, the bottom share falls to 4% and the top share falls to 40%. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both groups lose income because both shares fall.
Bottom income falls from $5 million to $4.8 million; top income rises from $45 million to $48 million despite its smaller share.
Both groups gain income because total income rises.
Bottom income rises to $6 million and top income falls to $40 million because shares should be applied to the original total.
q.feedback: Compute each group’s share of the corresponding total. Bottom: 0.05×100=5 versus 0.04×120=4.8. Top: 0.45×100=45 versus 0.40×120=48. A changing share does not by itself establish the change in dollars.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curve showing the bottom 40 percent receiving 15 percent of income.
q.graphDescription: The equality line is diagonal. The Lorenz curve passes through cumulative population-income points (20,5), (40,15), (60,30), (80,55), and (100,100); the bottom-40-percent reading is highlighted.
q.graphScenario: single Lorenz curve with quintile readings

key: Bottom income falls from $5 million to $4.8 million; top income rises from $45 million to $48 million despite its smaller share.

q.q: The graph’s Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252. Average real income also falls from $20,000 to $18,000. A report says the lower Gini proves higher living standards for every group. Which assessment is correct?
options: The Gini falls by 0.128, which proves every group’s real income rises despite the lower mean.
The Gini falls by 0.128 and average income by 10%; reduced relative inequality does not prove every group is better off.
The Gini rises by 0.128 because lower average income necessarily increases relative inequality.
The Gini falls by 12.8 income dollars per household, exactly offsetting the $2,000 income decline.
q.feedback: The Gini change is 0.380−0.252=0.128; mean income falls 2,000/20,000=10%. Distribution and income level must be assessed separately.
q.imageAlt: An after-policy Lorenz curve lies closer to equality than the before-policy curve; Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252.
q.graphDescription: Before-policy cumulative income shares are 5, 15, 30, and 55 percent at cumulative populations 20, 40, 60, and 80 percent. After-policy shares are 10, 22, 40, and 65 percent. The stated Gini coefficients are 0.380 before and 0.252 after.
q.graphScenario: before-and-after Lorenz curves with Gini values

key: The Gini falls by 0.128 and average income by 10%; reduced relative inequality does not prove every group is better off.

q.q: At the 40% population point, the graph gives cumulative income of 15%. A student reports a Gini of 0.25 by subtracting 0.15 from 0.40. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The Gini is 0.25 because every pointwise vertical gap equals the entire inequality area.
The 25-percentage-point gap is valid at that point, but Gini depends on the area between the entire Lorenz curve and equality.
The correct Gini is 0.55 because cumulative income and population shares should be added.
The gap is 15 percentage points because the equality line is horizontal at 30%.
q.feedback: The pointwise gap is 40−15=25 percentage points. It is one height, not the area-based Gini; the rest of the distribution matters.
q.imageAlt: Lorenz curve showing the bottom 40 percent receiving 15 percent of income.
q.graphDescription: The equality line is diagonal. The Lorenz curve passes through cumulative population-income points (20,5), (40,15), (60,30), (80,55), and (100,100); the bottom-40-percent reading is highlighted.
q.graphScenario: single Lorenz curve with quintile readings

key: The 25-percentage-point gap is valid at that point, but Gini depends on the area between the entire Lorenz curve and equality.

q.q: Initially the top quintile receives 45% of income and the bottom quintile 5%. A policy shifts five percentage points of total income from the top to the bottom, with total income and rankings unchanged. What happens to the top-to-bottom share ratio?
options: It falls from 9 to 8 because transferring five percentage points changes the ratio by one.
It falls from 9 to 4, but this change alone does not establish how much the entire distribution’s Gini changes.
It rises from 9 to 10 because the bottom share rises to 10%.
It stays at 9 because transfers cannot change relative income shares.
q.feedback: The original ratio is 45/5=9. New shares are 40% and 10%, giving 40/10=4. The full Lorenz distribution is needed for the Gini change.

key: It falls from 9 to 4, but this change alone does not establish how much the entire distribution’s Gini changes.

q.q: The top quintile initially receives nine times the bottom quintile’s share: 45% versus 5%. A policy keeps their combined 50% share fixed but aims for a ratio of four. Which new shares meet both conditions?
options: Top 36%, bottom 9%; the ratio is four and their combined share remains 50%.
Top 40%, bottom 10%; shift five percentage points from top to bottom.
Top 45%, bottom 11.25%; preserve the top share and the original combined share.
Top 25%, bottom 25%; equal shares give a ratio of four.
q.feedback: Let the bottom share be b and the top 4b. Their sum is 5b=50%, so b=10% and top=40%. Both the target ratio and the combined-share constraint must hold.

key: Top 40%, bottom 10%; shift five percentage points from top to bottom.

q.q: Distribution A’s Lorenz curve lies everywhere above B’s and below equality. A has mean income $15,000 and B $25,000. Which judgment is supported without imposing an equity preference?
options: A has less relative inequality, so every household in A must have a higher real income than its counterpart in B.
B has less relative inequality because its mean income is higher.
The two distributions have identical inequality because both Lorenz curves end at 100%.
A has less relative inequality, but its lower mean prevents concluding from Lorenz dominance alone that its households have higher real incomes.
q.feedback: Lorenz dominance ranks relative inequality, not income levels. A’s higher curve and lower mean can coexist; the welfare comparison needs more information or explicit value judgments.

key: A has less relative inequality, but its lower mean prevents concluding from Lorenz dominance alone that its households have higher real incomes.

q.q: A person values avoiding a $20 loss more strongly than obtaining a $20 gain relative to the same reference point. Which pattern is illustrated?
options: Risk neutrality
Loss aversion
Availability from a vivid recent event
Perfectly symmetric valuation of gains and losses
q.feedback: The comparison holds the amount fixed and shows greater weight on a loss relative to the reference point.

key: Loss aversion

q.q: Hidden quality makes buyers offer $80 for a pooled device. Good sellers require at least $100; bad sellers require $30. Which sellers are willing to trade at the pooled price?
options: Good sellers only
Both types
Neither type
Bad sellers only
q.feedback: The $80 offer exceeds the bad seller’s reservation value but falls below the good seller’s. This selection can worsen the pool.

key: Bad sellers only

q.q: Before buying a warranty, a customer privately knows its device is fragile. Which fact would instead describe moral hazard?
options: The customer knew the device was fragile before contracting.
The customer handles the device less carefully after obtaining coverage.
The warranty price is printed in the contract.
The seller sees the same fragility test as the customer.
q.feedback: Hidden preexisting fragility creates adverse selection; changed care after coverage is a behavioral response creating moral hazard.

key: The customer handles the device less carefully after obtaining coverage.

q.q: A seller can purchase credible quality certification for $5. It raises the price a verified good device receives from $80 to $100. Holding all other costs fixed, is certification privately worthwhile for that seller?
options: No; any positive verification fee makes certification unprofitable.
Yes; the seller gains the entire $100 as additional profit.
No; the price gain is only $5.
Yes; the $20 price gain exceeds the $5 fee by $15.
q.feedback: Certification adds $20 to revenue and $5 to cost, for a $15 net gain.

key: Yes; the $20 price gain exceeds the $5 fee by $15.

q.q: An insurer reimburses all losses. It then adds a deductible that makes the insured bear part of each loss, holding information and all other terms fixed. Which incentive changes most directly?
options: The insured bears a smaller loss and therefore has less reason for care.
The insured has a stronger financial reason to prevent a loss.
The insurer learns every hidden characteristic before contracting.
The deductible guarantees no accident can occur.
