q.feedback: A deductible leaves some loss with the insured and can strengthen care incentives, without guaranteeing perfect care or revealing all types.

key: The insured has a stronger financial reason to prevent a loss.

q.q: An insured driver maintains exactly the same level of care before and after coverage. An accident then occurs. Does that accident alone establish moral hazard?
options: Yes; every insured loss proves reduced care.
Yes; the insurer’s payment establishes hidden precontract risk.
No; moral hazard is impossible in insurance.
No; the accident alone does not demonstrate a coverage-induced change in behavior.
q.feedback: A bad outcome can occur without a change in incentives or behavior. The stated unchanged care does not demonstrate moral hazard.

key: No; the accident alone does not demonstrate a coverage-induced change in behavior.

q.q: A job applicant independently obtains a credible certificate before approaching employers. Employers did not require or design a menu of choices. Which information mechanism is described?
options: Screening by the employer
Moral hazard after employment
A benefits cliff
Signaling by the informed applicant
q.feedback: The informed side takes an observable action to communicate its type.

key: Signaling by the informed applicant

q.q: An informed seller voluntarily posts a warranty that is much more expensive for low-quality sellers to honor. Why can it convey quality?
options: All sellers face identical warranty costs and incentives.
Low-quality sellers may find imitation less profitable because expected warranty costs are higher.
Posting a warranty mechanically improves the physical product.
A warranty prevents buyers from learning about defects.
q.feedback: Different expected costs can make the observable warranty a credible signal rather than cheap talk.

key: Low-quality sellers may find imitation less profitable because expected warranty costs are higher.

q.q: Workers are randomly assigned to automatic retirement enrollment or active enrollment, with identical plans and easy opt-out. Participation is 80% versus 50%. What does this comparison most directly support?
options: The default changes every worker’s income.
All automatically enrolled workers prefer the plan to every alternative.
The plan’s financial return differs by 30 percentage points.
The enrollment default affects participation in this setting.
q.feedback: Random assignment and identical terms isolate the default difference. Participation alone does not establish each worker’s welfare or financial return.

key: The enrollment default affects participation in this setting.

q.q: A behavioral intervention was tested only on volunteers from one workplace. Which statement accurately describes the evidence?
options: It proves effectiveness in every workplace.
It provides evidence about that sample; broader effectiveness needs additional support.
It supplies no evidence because volunteers are never informative.
It establishes the intervention’s mechanism solely from the sample size.
q.feedback: A restricted sample can be informative while limiting generalization to other settings.

key: It provides evidence about that sample; broader effectiveness needs additional support.

q.q: A voting rule ranks A above B. Voters’ individual comparisons of A with B stay fixed, but changing their views about C makes the social ranking put B above A. Which condition is violated?
options: The requirement that voters have no preferences
Independence of irrelevant alternatives
A rule requiring equal incomes
The arithmetic of vote totals only
q.feedback: IIA requires the social comparison of A and B to depend on individual comparisons of that pair, not changed views about a third option.

key: Independence of irrelevant alternatives

q.q: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Which option wins a pairwise contest between A and B?
options: B by two groups to one
A unanimously
They tie
A by two groups to one
q.feedback: The first and third groups prefer A to B; only the second prefers B.

key: A by two groups to one

q.q: Applicants all know their own risk before applying. Which policy most directly addresses adverse selection?
options: Monitoring precautions taken after coverage begins
Reimbursing every claim without inspection
Credible precontract risk verification
Hiding all application information from the insurer
q.feedback: Adverse selection concerns hidden precontract types. Risk verification addresses that timing, whereas monitoring later behavior addresses moral hazard.

key: Credible precontract risk verification

q.q: Coverage is priced separately for each applicant’s accurately verified risk, with no hidden risk characteristic in this model. Does a high-risk person buying insurance alone demonstrate adverse selection?
options: Yes; any high-risk purchase proves private information exists.
Yes; risk-based pricing hides the applicant’s risk.
No; high risk is observed and incorporated in pricing.
No; high-risk people cannot benefit from insurance.
q.feedback: Adverse selection requires an information problem affecting selection. A high-risk purchase at a fully informed price is not sufficient evidence.

key: No; high risk is observed and incorporated in pricing.

q.q: A buyer values a good device at $120 and a bad device at $40. Half of devices offered are each type, but quality is hidden. What is the risk-neutral buyer’s expected value?
q.feedback: Expected value is 0.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 40 = $80. Pooling quality makes willingness to pay depend on the mix.

q.q: After good devices withdraw from a market, only devices worth $40 to buyers remain. Buyers learn the new composition. Should their former $80 pooled valuation persist?
options: Yes; the original mix determines value permanently.
No; the withdrawal raises expected value to $120.
No; the remaining pool is worth $40 per device.
Yes; observed composition cannot affect willingness to pay.
q.feedback: Once buyers know only bad devices remain, the old mixed-pool expectation is no longer appropriate.

key: No; the remaining pool is worth $40 per device.

q.q: Two banks hold identical assets initially. Only one receives a credible promise that taxpayers will absorb large future losses. With other incentives fixed, which response is consistent with moral hazard?
options: The protected bank selects less risk because it bears all taxpayers’ losses.
Both banks must select identical risk because their initial assets match.
The unprotected bank becomes insured merely because another bank is protected.
The protected bank selects more risk because it bears less downside.
q.feedback: The guarantee changes the protected bank’s marginal exposure to losses even though initial assets are equal.

key: The protected bank selects more risk because it bears less downside.

q.q: Monitoring costs $8 per policy and is expected to reduce real accident losses by $5, with no other benefits or costs. Is monitoring justified by net resource savings in this example?
options: Yes; every reduction in moral hazard exceeds its cost.
No; it costs $3 more than the expected loss reduction.
Yes; the net saving is $13.
No; the reduction in losses is a transfer rather than a resource benefit.
q.feedback: The resource gain is $5 and the cost is $8, giving net savings of −$3.

key: No; it costs $3 more than the expected loss reduction.

q.q: An employer offers two contract packages that induce applicants with different private productivity to choose differently. Who designs the information-revealing action, and what is it called?
options: The informed applicant designs screening.
The uninformed employer sends a signal of applicant quality.
The applicants disclose all types through a compulsory public test.
The uninformed employer designs screening.
q.feedback: Screening is initiated by the less-informed side through offers that reveal private information via choices.

key: The uninformed employer designs screening.

q.q: A bank offers borrowers a choice between a low-interest loan with collateral and a high-interest loan without collateral. Borrowers privately know their repayment risk. Which action constitutes screening?
options: A borrower’s unsolicited public reputation campaign
The bank’s design of the contract menu
The bank’s payment after a default
A borrower’s change in effort after the loan
q.feedback: The uninformed bank designs alternatives intended to reveal risk through borrowers’ choices.

key: The bank’s design of the contract menu

q.q: After seeing a vivid news report of a rare accident, a traveler raises its estimated frequency without new statistical data. What is the availability-based explanation?
options: The report mechanically changes the true accident rate.
The traveler computes the rate from a larger random sample.
The traveler values losses and gains symmetrically.
Ease of recalling the event substitutes for evidence about its frequency.
q.feedback: Salient, easy-to-recall examples can receive excessive weight when judging frequency.

key: Ease of recalling the event substitutes for evidence about its frequency.

q.q: Five voters have single-peaked preferences over one spending level, with ideal points 1, 3, 4, 8 and 10. Which level is the median ideal point and defeats any alternative in pairwise majority voting under these assumptions?
q.feedback: The ordered middle ideal point is 4, not the mean 5.2. Single-peakedness makes the median proposal a majority winner.

q.q: Buyers initially think 75% of devices are good, worth $120, and 25% are bad, worth $40. Good sellers require $90. If the good share falls to 50%, how does participation change at expected-value prices?
options: The offer rises from $80 to $100, attracting good sellers.
The offer falls from $120 to $40, but good sellers still accept.
The offer stays at $90 because reservation values determine expected quality.
The offer falls from $100 to $80, causing good sellers to withdraw.
q.feedback: The initial expectation is 0.75(120)+0.25(40)=$100; the new expectation is $80, below the good seller’s $90 reservation value.

key: The offer falls from $100 to $80, causing good sellers to withdraw.

q.q: A warranty provider introduces a reliable pre-purchase fragility test but does not monitor care after purchase. Which problem does this change directly address?
options: Postpurchase moral hazard, while fragility remains hidden.
Adverse selection from hidden fragility, while postpurchase moral hazard can remain.
Both problems completely, because any test makes behavior enforceable.
Neither problem, because information never affects contracting.
q.feedback: The test reveals precontract type; it does not reveal or change the enforceability of later care.

key: Adverse selection from hidden fragility, while postpurchase moral hazard can remain.

q.q: An insurer can perfectly verify a driver’s care but cannot contract on or enforce consequences for that care. Does observation alone remove the incentive to take less care?
options: Yes; seeing an action automatically changes the driver’s payoff.
Yes; observation refunds every premium.
No; the remaining issue must be hidden precontract type only.
No; an observable action need not be contractible, so incentives may remain unchanged.
q.feedback: Observation and enforceability are separate. Verified actions need enforceable consequences to change the described incentive.

key: No; an observable action need not be contractible, so incentives may remain unchanged.

q.q: A small study reports that a reminder improves saving. A larger, preregistered replication with comparable conditions finds an estimate near zero and a confidence interval excluding the original large effect. What is the best response?
options: Discard the replication because it disagrees with the first result.
Reduce confidence in the original large effect while considering both studies’ uncertainty and designs.
Conclude reminders must reduce saving in every setting.
Treat the first estimate as certain because it was published first.
q.feedback: The replication supplies contrary evidence about the claimed magnitude. It need not prove an exactly zero effect everywhere to weaken the original claim.

key: Reduce confidence in the original large effect while considering both studies’ uncertainty and designs.

q.q: A program switches its default at the same time it increases the employer subsidy. Participation rises. Why can the increase not be attributed entirely to the default from this comparison alone?
options: Defaults cannot influence behavior when a subsidy exists.
Participation is unrelated to incentives.
An increase in participation proves the subsidy had no effect.
The subsidy changed too, creating a competing explanation.
q.feedback: Two relevant conditions changed together. Without further evidence their contributions cannot be separated.

key: The subsidy changed too, creating a competing explanation.

q.q: Two studies estimate an intervention effect at 4 and 5 percentage points, each with an uncertainty interval from −2 to 10. Does the one-point difference establish conflicting effects?
options: Yes; any different point estimates establish different underlying effects.
No; the estimates are close relative to their reported uncertainty.
Yes; overlapping intervals prove opposite mechanisms.
No; the true effect is necessarily exactly 4.5 points.
q.feedback: Sampling variation can produce nearby estimates. Their uncertainty does not support treating the one-point difference as a demonstrated conflict.

key: No; the estimates are close relative to their reported uncertainty.

q.q: A person rejects a fair gamble. Why does that fact alone not establish loss aversion?
options: Loss aversion requires accepting every fair gamble.
Ordinary risk aversion can also explain rejection; evidence about gains and losses around a reference point is needed.
Risk aversion and loss aversion are identical definitions.
Rejecting a gamble proves probability judgments are accurate.
q.feedback: Risk aversion concerns curvature over outcomes; loss aversion concerns asymmetric valuation of gains and losses relative to a reference point. A single rejection need not distinguish them.

key: Ordinary risk aversion can also explain rejection; evidence about gains and losses around a reference point is needed.

q.q: Two groups see the same accident-rate table; one also sees a vivid anecdote. Random assignment yields higher risk estimates only in the anecdote group. What does this design add?
options: It proves the true accident rate rose in the anecdote group.
It changes the table’s sample size for one group.
It establishes loss aversion rather than a judgment effect.
It isolates the anecdote’s effect while holding the statistical information fixed.
q.feedback: Holding the table constant and randomly varying the anecdote supports an effect of salience on risk judgment.

key: It isolates the anecdote’s effect while holding the statistical information fixed.

q.q: A rule violates independence of irrelevant alternatives in one example. Does that alone imply that every voter’s ranking is cyclic?
options: Yes; IIA is the definition of individual transitivity.
No; the collective rule can violate IIA even when each individual ranking is transitive.
Yes; adding an alternative necessarily changes every pairwise preference.
No; IIA places no restriction on a social ranking rule.
q.feedback: IIA concerns how a collective pairwise ranking responds to preference profiles; it is distinct from consistency of each individual’s ranking.

key: No; the collective rule can violate IIA even when each individual ranking is transitive.

q.q: After a recent burglary, residents become more worried. Local data also show a sustained increase in burglaries. Why is increased concern alone insufficient to diagnose availability bias?
options: A recent event prevents any rational response.
Availability bias requires no memorable events.
Statistical evidence cannot influence perceived risk.
The concern could reflect the documented increase in risk as well as the vivid event.
q.feedback: A changed belief is not automatically a bias when relevant risk evidence also changes. The two explanations require discrimination.

key: The concern could reflect the documented increase in risk as well as the vivid event.

q.q: Sellers claim their products are reliable. An independent test accurately identifies reliability and results are disclosed before buyers choose. Which mechanism could improve trade?
options: The test changes every unreliable product into a reliable one.
The test prevents all buyers from considering prices.
The test creates adverse selection by hiding quality that was formerly disclosed.
Reliable sellers can distinguish their products, reducing buyers’ need to price all products as a pooled average.
q.feedback: Credible disclosure separates qualities rather than improving the physical product itself; good products need not be priced as though they were average.

key: Reliable sellers can distinguish their products, reducing buyers’ need to price all products as a pooled average.

q.q: Two warranty markets differ only in information. In A, fragility is privately known before purchase; in B, fragility is verified and priced, but postpurchase care is unobserved. Which pairing is correct?
options: A: moral hazard; B: adverse selection
A: adverse selection; B: moral hazard
Both: adverse selection only
Both: moral hazard only
q.feedback: A concerns who selects coverage based on hidden type. B concerns hidden actions after coverage begins.

key: A: adverse selection; B: moral hazard

q.q: A bank expects rescue only if its losses become very large. Managers respond by choosing a riskier portfolio after financing is obtained. What makes this a moral-hazard mechanism?
options: The rescue reveals the bank’s hidden precontract type with certainty.
The risk increase is a fixed characteristic that cannot respond to incentives.
Rescue expectations raise the bank’s share of every possible loss.
The rescue expectation reduces the downside the bank bears and changes its later risk-taking.
q.feedback: Sharing or shifting losses can weaken incentives to avoid them; the stated change is in behavior after financing.

key: The rescue expectation reduces the downside the bank bears and changes its later risk-taking.

q.q: A borrower offers collateral as a signal of repayment confidence. Suppose both high-risk and low-risk borrowers face the same expected collateral loss and obtain the same loan benefit. What follows?
options: Collateral necessarily separates types even when their incentives match.
The stated costs and benefits do not give the two types different signaling incentives.
Equal incentives reveal every borrower to be low risk.
Equal incentives convert the signal into perfect lender screening.
q.feedback: A separating signal needs an incentive difference that makes mimicking unattractive for one type. The stated identical payoffs provide none.

key: The stated costs and benefits do not give the two types different signaling incentives.

q.q: A warranty initially costs good sellers $2 and bad sellers $20 to honor. Third-party insurance then makes the warranty cost $3 for either type. Holding the price premium fixed, what happens to its separating rationale?
options: It strengthens because identical costs reveal quality more accurately.
It weakens because the warranty no longer imposes a higher signaling cost on bad sellers.
It is unchanged because signaling never depends on imitation incentives.
It reverses physical quality, making bad products good.
q.feedback: Equalizing the cost removes the original reason bad sellers would be less willing to mimic the warranty.

key: It weakens because the warranty no longer imposes a higher signaling cost on bad sellers.

q.q: Automatic enrollment raises participation, but some workers later opt out and report that the plan did not fit their needs. Which conclusion follows?
options: The opt-outs prove defaults have no effect on initial choices.
Higher participation establishes unanimous informed preference for the plan.
The plan must yield lower returns solely because opt-outs occur.
The default changes choices; higher participation alone does not establish that every affected worker benefits.
q.feedback: Choice effects and welfare effects are separate. Some people may remain enrolled because of inertia rather than a plan that best fits their circumstances.

key: The default changes choices; higher participation alone does not establish that every affected worker benefits.

q.q: A trial finds that a default raises participation by 20 points among new employees. A firm plans to apply the same estimate to long-serving workers who already made active choices. What limitation matters?
options: Random assignment guarantees an identical effect in every population.
Prior choices make the trial’s result mathematically impossible.
A 20-point effect means participation must double in every group.
The trial identifies an effect for its participants; transfer to a group with prior active choices requires evidence.
q.feedback: Internal evidence from one group does not guarantee the same response in a different decision context.

key: The trial identifies an effect for its participants; transfer to a group with prior active choices requires evidence.

q.q: Two identical outcomes are framed as keeping $80 of an endowed $100 or losing $20 of it. A decision changes with the framing. Which explanation is consistent with this evidence, without claiming it is uniquely proven?
options: The frames produce different final wealth by definition.
Reference-dependent evaluation can make the loss frame more salient despite identical final wealth.
The change proves the person has different income in the two descriptions.
The frames eliminate any role for a reference point.
q.feedback: The monetary outcome is the same. A difference in response is consistent with framing and reference dependence, though it alone does not uniquely identify a mechanism.

key: Reference-dependent evaluation can make the loss frame more salient despite identical final wealth.

q.q: A policy analyst predicts that a $50 rebate framed as avoiding a loss will work identically for people who expected the rebate and people who did not. What does reference dependence suggest?
options: Equal dollars force identical reference points.
Different expectations may create different reference points, so equal dollars need not produce equal responses.
Only the final dollar amount can matter in a reference-dependent model.
A reference point changes the legal value of the currency.
q.feedback: Expectations can affect whether an outcome is experienced as a gain or avoidance of a loss, limiting the prediction of identical responses.

key: Different expectations may create different reference points, so equal dollars need not produce equal responses.

q.q: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Under sequential pairwise voting with sincere votes, compare agenda 1 (A versus B, then the winner versus C) with agenda 2 (B versus C, then the winner versus A).
options: Both agendas select A.
Agenda 1 selects B; agenda 2 selects C.
Both agendas select C.
Agenda 1 selects C; agenda 2 selects A.
q.feedback: A beats B but then loses to C. B beats C but then loses to A. The cycle makes the final result depend on the agenda.

key: Agenda 1 selects C; agenda 2 selects A.

q.q: A median-voter prediction was derived for single-peaked preferences on one policy dimension. The election then adds a second independent policy dimension. What conclusion is warranted?
options: The arithmetic median on the first dimension must still win every multidimensional comparison.
Adding a dimension guarantees unanimous agreement.
The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.
All individual preferences must become cyclic.
q.feedback: The one-dimensional ordering supports the median-voter result. Moving to multiple dimensions removes that guarantee without proving that a cycle must occur.

key: The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.

q.q: High-productivity applicants value a job at $30,000 more than their alternative and face a $5,000 certificate cost. Low-productivity applicants gain $10,000 and face a $15,000 cost. With the job available only to certificate holders, can certification separate the two types under these payoffs?
options: No; both types gain because the job is valuable.
No; both types lose because certification is costly.
Yes; low types gain $5,000 while high types lose $25,000.
Yes; high types gain $25,000 net while low types would lose $5,000.
q.feedback: High types have benefit minus cost 30,000 − 5,000 = 25,000; low types have 10,000 − 15,000 = −5,000. Their incentives differ as separation requires.

key: Yes; high types gain $25,000 net while low types would lose $5,000.

q.q: Several small studies report a large behavioral effect, while a well-designed large replication reports a smaller positive effect. Which conclusion best combines magnitude and replication evidence?
options: Any smaller effect proves the underlying mechanism does not exist.
The evidence may support a positive effect while weakening the claim that it is as large as first reported.
A positive effect in the replication confirms the original magnitude exactly.
The number of small studies alone makes sample size and design irrelevant.
q.feedback: Replicating a direction does not establish the original magnitude. Assessing both size and uncertainty can support a more modest conclusion.

key: The evidence may support a positive effect while weakening the claim that it is as large as first reported.

q.q: A vivid report raises perceived accident risk, while a large representative dataset shows that the rate has not changed. Which response most directly corrects an availability-based inference?
options: Increase the estimated frequency further because the story is memorable.
Ignore both the story and the dataset because no probability can be estimated.
Treat the single report as more representative than the large dataset.
Use the representative frequency data while distinguishing vividness from prevalence.
q.feedback: Representative base-rate evidence addresses frequency; vividness alone does not show a change in that frequency.

key: Use the representative frequency data while distinguishing vividness from prevalence.

q.q: A designer claims that Arrow’s theorem proves no useful election rule can exist. Which correction best states the limitation of that claim?
options: The theorem guarantees all voting rules satisfy every fairness condition.
The theorem concerns satisfying a specified set of conditions together; a rule can remain useful while relaxing a condition.
The theorem applies only when there are exactly two alternatives.
The theorem says individual preferences cannot be transitive.
q.feedback: An impossibility result about jointly meeting conditions is not a claim that every rule is useless. Practical design involves which conditions to retain or relax.

key: The theorem concerns satisfying a specified set of conditions together; a rule can remain useful while relaxing a condition.

q.q: A reminder works in one experiment but not in another. The second changes both the population and delivery method. Which follow-up best distinguishes these explanations?
options: Repeat the original treatment only and ignore the second population.
Vary population and delivery method separately in a design that can compare their effects.
Average the two results and declare the mechanism universal.
Attribute the difference to population without testing delivery.
q.feedback: Separating the factors can reveal whether population, delivery or their interaction explains the difference; the two-study comparison confounds them.

key: Vary population and delivery method separately in a design that can compare their effects.

q.q: A marketplace makes product quality observable before purchase and makes seller effort observable and enforceable after purchase. Pollution from production still harms nearby residents. Which assessment separates the problems?
options: Better information removes the pollution cost as well as the hidden-information problems, so no other distortion remains.
Only hidden action can be addressed; observing quality before purchase cannot affect selection into trade.
Better information can reduce hidden-type and hidden-action problems, but it does not itself make sellers bear the pollution cost.
Only pollution can be addressed; making information shared cannot improve the contracting problems.
q.feedback: Observable quality improves type-based contracting; enforceable effort improves action incentives. Pollution is an external cost, so it can remain even when information is shared.

key: Better information can reduce hidden-type and hidden-action problems, but it does not itself make sellers bear the pollution cost.

q.q: A used-device seller knows the battery fails after an hour; buyers cannot test it before paying. Which information is asymmetric?
options: The device’s hidden quality before the transaction
A buyer’s effort after purchasing insurance
Both parties’ knowledge of the posted price
The number of units in a public inventory
q.feedback: The seller knows a quality characteristic the buyer cannot observe before buying.

key: The device’s hidden quality before the transaction

q.q: Two borrowers seek identical loans, but only they know their project risks before signing. A lender charges a pooled interest rate. Safer borrowers increasingly decline the loans, while riskier borrowers remain. Which diagnosis and response fit the timing?
options: Moral hazard worsens the borrower pool; monitoring effort only after lending directly reveals the original hidden types.
Adverse selection worsens the borrower pool; verified pre-loan risk information can support risk-specific offers.
Adverse selection improves the pool; increasing the pooled rate must bring safer borrowers back.
Moral hazard improves the pool; a uniform rate removes differences in project risk before contracting.
q.feedback: Private risk is a hidden type before the contract. If safer borrowers exit, the remaining pool becomes riskier; screening before lending targets that mechanism.

key: Adverse selection worsens the borrower pool; verified pre-loan risk information can support risk-specific offers.

q.q: Both sides can verify a product’s quality and enforce promised actions, but only the seller knows its private reservation price. Which statement is correct?
options: All private information is eliminated because quality is verifiable.
Enforceable actions necessarily create moral hazard.
Quality and action problems have been addressed, but the parties need not have identical information about valuations.
Private reservation prices imply the product’s quality cannot be verified.
q.feedback: Information about quality, actions and valuations are different. Removing two asymmetries does not logically eliminate the third.

key: Quality and action problems have been addressed, but the parties need not have identical information about valuations.

q.q: A buyer and seller both receive a reliable independent inspection of a device before trading. Does the seller’s former private knowledge of battery quality remain an information advantage for this transaction?
options: No; the verified inspection makes that quality information available to both.
Yes; any sale necessarily contains hidden quality.
Yes; verification creates postpurchase moral hazard.
No; inspection guarantees the absence of all market failures.
q.feedback: Reliable shared quality information removes this particular asymmetry, without establishing that every other market failure is absent.

key: No; the verified inspection makes that quality information available to both.

q.q: Buyers value a verified reliable product at $120, and its seller’s resource cost is $100. Without verification, buyers offer only $80 because quality is hidden. Independent verification costs $10 and reliably identifies quality. Which conclusion follows?
options: Verification cannot restore trade because the original pooled offer is below the seller’s cost.
Verification restores trade and creates $40 of net gains, measured by the rise from the pooled offer to buyer value.
Verification leaves $20 of net gains because a real verification cost is only a transfer.
Verification can restore the reliable-product trade and leave $10 of net gains after its resource cost.
q.feedback: Without verification the $80 offer cannot cover the reliable seller’s $100 cost. With verification, willingness to pay $120 exceeds cost $100 plus verification $10, leaving $10 of net surplus.

key: Verification can restore the reliable-product trade and leave $10 of net gains after its resource cost.

q.q: A borrower knows its intended project is risky, but the lender sees only the same application data used for safer borrowers. At which point does this asymmetry arise?
options: Before the loan contract, when the borrower’s type is hidden.
Only after the borrower misses a repayment.
Only when the lender posts an interest rate.
After repayment, when the loan is no longer active.
q.feedback: The private project-risk information exists before contracting; an eventual loss is not needed for the asymmetry to exist.

key: Before the loan contract, when the borrower’s type is hidden.

q.q: Before lending, a bank can verify a borrower’s past defaults but cannot observe the risk of its new project. What can the bank conclude about information asymmetry?
options: All private information disappears once any history is verified.
One source has been reduced, but private information about the new project can remain.
Verification creates hidden past defaults that were previously observable.
The remaining problem must concern actions taken after the loan, not hidden current project quality.
q.feedback: Verifying one observable history does not reveal every relevant private characteristic. The new project’s risk remains hidden before contracting.

key: One source has been reduced, but private information about the new project can remain.

q.q: A buyer and contractor can observe quality but cannot enforce a promised effort level in court. A proposal merely publishes the observed effort, while another makes payment contingent on a verified effort measure. Which is more directly targeted at hidden-action incentives?
options: Publication alone, because observing an action necessarily makes all promised penalties enforceable.
Neither, because incentives matter only for hidden types before contracting.
The contingent-payment contract, because shared observation must be connected to enforceable rewards or penalties to change the contractor’s payoff.
The contingent-payment contract only if it prevents buyers from observing quality.
q.feedback: Information and enforceability are distinct. Making payment contingent on a verified action changes the incentive to exert effort; observation alone does not establish that contractual consequence.

key: The contingent-payment contract, because shared observation must be connected to enforceable rewards or penalties to change the contractor’s payoff.

q.q: A verification service reveals product quality only after a sale becomes final, with no refund rights. Why might it fail to prevent a buyer’s initial quality mistake?
options: Verified information can never influence choice.
The service necessarily changes the product’s production cost.
The buyer had full information before purchasing.
The information arrives too late to affect the irreversible purchase choice.
q.feedback: Timing matters: postpurchase knowledge cannot guide the already irreversible decision described.

key: The information arrives too late to affect the irreversible purchase choice.

q.q: Half of used devices are reliable and worth $120 to buyers; half are defective and worth $40. Reliable sellers require at least $100 and defective sellers $20. Buyers cannot distinguish quality. What happens if they initially offer the expected value and then update after sellers decide whether to participate?
options: The initial offer is $80; reliable sellers stay because $80 exceeds defective sellers’ $20 requirement.
The initial offer is $160; both types stay because values should be added without weighting.
The initial offer is $100; defective sellers withdraw because buyers prefer reliable products.
The initial offer is $80; reliable sellers withdraw, so the remaining pool supports only $40.
q.feedback: The pooled value is 0.5×120+0.5×40=$80. That is below reliable sellers’ $100 reservation value. Their exit leaves defective products valued at $40, illustrating adverse selection.

key: The initial offer is $80; reliable sellers withdraw, so the remaining pool supports only $40.

q.q: An insurer must charge one premium. People who privately know they face unusually low risk stop buying after the premium rises. What happens to the average risk among those remaining?
options: It falls.
It must stay fixed.
It rises.
It becomes zero.
q.feedback: The withdrawal of safer customers leaves a larger share of high-risk customers in the insured pool.

key: It rises.

q.q: Customers privately know device fragility before buying insurance; after purchase some reduce care. The insurer proposes a durability test before purchase and a deductible on each claim. Which assessment correctly separates the purposes?
options: The test addresses moral hazard after purchase; the deductible identifies the device’s original hidden type without affecting care.
The test addresses hidden type and adverse selection; the deductible can preserve care incentives after purchase and reduce moral hazard.
Both target only adverse selection because all insurance problems arise before purchase.
Both target only moral hazard because private fragility is an action chosen after purchase.
q.feedback: Fragility at purchase is a type; care after coverage is an action. Screening and cost sharing address distinct information and incentive problems.

key: The test addresses hidden type and adverse selection; the deductible can preserve care incentives after purchase and reduce moral hazard.

q.q: A lender cannot observe applicants’ existing risk types. After the pooled rate rises, low-risk applicants withdraw; among those funded, some also switch to riskier projects that the lender cannot monitor. Which policy pairing addresses both mechanisms?
options: Screen applicants’ types before lending and assume that this alone makes later actions observable.
Screen applicants’ types before lending and link repayment incentives or monitoring to post-loan actions.
Monitor funded borrowers’ actions and assume that this alone identifies the risk of applicants who withdrew.
Raise the pooled rate again and treat both changes as evidence that all applicants have the same risk.
q.feedback: Safe-type withdrawal is adverse selection; changing risk after funding is moral hazard. The two stages call for information about types and incentives for actions, respectively.

key: Screen applicants’ types before lending and link repayment incentives or monitoring to post-loan actions.

q.q: A pooled used-product market loses reliable sellers because buyers cannot distinguish quality. A manufacturer proposes a warranty that is cheap for reliable products but expensive for unreliable ones because claims are verifiable. Why can this help, and what condition matters?
options: The warranty can credibly signal quality whenever it is advertised, even if both seller types can imitate it at the same cost.
The warranty solves post-purchase buyer moral hazard by making the original product type identical across sellers.
The warranty eliminates the need for credibility because buyers can infer quality from a higher asking price alone.
The warranty can credibly signal quality if expected claim costs make imitation unattractive for unreliable sellers.
q.feedback: A warranty is informative when seller types face different expected costs and the claim promise is enforceable. If low-quality sellers can mimic it cheaply, the separating signal breaks down.

key: The warranty can credibly signal quality if expected claim costs make imitation unattractive for unreliable sellers.

q.q: Reliable products are worth $120 to buyers and cost sellers $100. Hidden quality prevents reliable sellers from trading at the pooled offer. Verification perfectly reveals quality but uses $30 of real resources per product. Is restoring each reliable trade with this verification method necessarily a surplus gain?
options: Yes; any trade restored by better information raises surplus regardless of verification cost.
Yes; the full $120 buyer value is a surplus gain because seller cost is a transfer.
No; verification prevents buyers from distinguishing reliable and defective products.
No; the potential $20 gain from trade is smaller than the $30 verification cost.
q.feedback: Better information can restore exchange, but here net surplus would be $120−$100−$30=−$10. The information improvement must be assessed alongside its resource cost.

key: No; the potential $20 gain from trade is smaller than the $30 verification cost.

q.q: An insurer can cheaply monitor care and enforce a premium discount for verified care, but cannot observe a customer’s inherited risk before contracting. Which problem can the policy directly reduce, and which may remain?
options: It can reduce adverse selection; moral hazard must remain even with enforceable care incentives.
It can reduce hidden-action moral hazard; hidden-type adverse selection may remain.
It eliminates both problems because monitoring later care reveals inherited risk perfectly.
It eliminates neither problem because premiums cannot change behavior.
q.feedback: A discount conditional on care changes the reward for a post-contract action. It does not, under the stated information limit, reveal the customer’s original risk type.

key: It can reduce hidden-action moral hazard; hidden-type adverse selection may remain.

q.q: A company can eliminate employees’ hidden shirking through monitoring. Monitoring would recover $18,000 of output but use $25,000 of real resources annually. A cheaper incentive contract recovers $12,000 at a $4,000 resource cost. Which comparison is correct?
options: Perfect monitoring gains $18,000 net and is preferable because its resource cost is irrelevant to incentives.
Perfect monitoring loses $7,000 net, while the incentive contract gains $8,000; eliminating all hidden action is not necessarily efficient.
The incentive contract loses $8,000 net because any remaining shirking makes a policy inefficient.
Both policies have the same net benefit because both address moral hazard.
q.feedback: Net benefits are 18,000−25,000=−7,000 and 12,000−4,000=8,000. Better observability is useful only when its gains justify its resource cost.

key: Perfect monitoring loses $7,000 net, while the incentive contract gains $8,000; eliminating all hidden action is not necessarily efficient.

q.q: An insurer offers low-premium/high-deductible and high-premium/low-deductible plans before it knows applicants’ risk types. A customer separately provides a costly certified safety record. Which distinction correctly identifies the two information mechanisms?
options: The menu is signaling by the informed insurer; the customer’s record is screening by the uninformed side.
Both are screening because neither depends on who initiates the information mechanism.
Both are moral hazard because the information concerns actions only after coverage begins.
The menu is screening by the less-informed insurer; the customer’s credible record is signaling by the informed side.
q.feedback: The insurer designs a menu to induce self-selection, a screening device. The informed applicant supplies a credible observable record, a signal. Timing and who initiates the mechanism distinguish them.

key: The menu is screening by the less-informed insurer; the customer’s credible record is signaling by the informed side.

q.q: A job applicant chooses to obtain an unsolicited certificate before applying; an employer separately offers a menu of trial contracts to reveal applicants’ types. Which action is signaling?
options: The applicant’s certificate
The employer’s contract menu
Both actions are signaling by the informed side.
Neither action can convey information.
q.feedback: The informed applicant initiates the certificate signal. The uninformed employer initiates the screening menu.

key: The applicant’s certificate

q.q: A crop price rises after a drought reduces harvests. A separate processing plant also discharges unpriced waste into a river. Which diagnosis and targeted response distinguish scarcity from market failure?
options: The crop price can signal genuine scarcity; a policy aimed at the waste should target its external cost rather than treating the high price alone as proof of failure.
Both are market failures solely because prices and waste increased, so a price ceiling necessarily corrects both.
Neither can be market failure because any outcome with a market price is efficient.
The drought is asymmetric information and the waste is merely a transfer between buyers and sellers.
q.commonError: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
q.feedback: A supply loss can raise a competitive price without creating a distortion. Unpriced harm omits social cost from the private decision and calls for a response to that specific wedge.

key: The crop price can signal genuine scarcity; a policy aimed at the waste should target its external cost rather than treating the high price alone as proof of failure.

q.q: Buyers cannot observe product risk before purchase. Mandatory disclosure accurately reports it, but only in a format most buyers cannot interpret. A simplified tested label helps buyers compare risks at lower reading cost. Which comparison is defensible?
options: Accurate disclosure necessarily eliminates the problem regardless of comprehension, so testing the label adds no information.
Both address an information problem, but the tested label can improve usable information more effectively; accuracy alone does not establish that the first format changes decisions.
The unreadable format solves an externality while the label creates monopoly power.
Neither addresses market failure because information costs cannot affect mutually beneficial trades.
q.feedback: The original problem is an information gap about risk. Disclosure must be usable to affect choices; evidence about comprehension and behavior distinguishes formal disclosure from an effective remedy.

key: Both address an information problem, but the tested label can improve usable information more effectively; accuracy alone does not establish that the first format changes decisions.

q.q: A corrective policy would prevent $120 of external harm while using $35 of compliance resources and $100 of administrative resources. A simpler policy prevents $80 of harm and uses $20 in total resources. Which recommendation follows from these estimates alone?
options: The full policy is preferable because it prevents more harm, regardless of implementation cost.
Both policies are equally desirable because each reduces a market failure.
The full policy has net benefit −$15 and the simpler policy +$60; the simpler remedy is preferable to both the full policy and doing nothing.
Doing nothing is preferable because any administrative cost makes intervention inefficient.
q.commonError: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
q.feedback: Net benefits are 120−35−100=−15 and 80−20=60. The scale of the original failure does not make every proposed correction worthwhile.

key: The full policy has net benefit −$15 and the simpler policy +$60; the simpler remedy is preferable to both the full policy and doing nothing.

q.q: A disclosure rule is forecast to prevent $90 of harm at $20 resource cost. A pilot finds that confusion causes $35 of additional harm and that only $50 of the original harm is actually prevented. A simpler label prevents $40 at $10 cost with no added confusion. Which comparison uses the observed performance?
options: The original rule has +$70 net benefit because forecasts should replace contradictory pilot evidence.
The original rule has +$30 net benefit because confusion is only a transfer, making it equivalent to the simpler label.
The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.
Neither can be compared because any information rule guarantees an efficient outcome.
q.commonError: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
q.feedback: Use the pilot’s actual effects: 50−35−20=−5. The alternative yields 40−10=30. The intended mechanism is relevant, but implementation evidence determines the net result.

key: The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.

q.q: A market maximizes measured total surplus but distributes it unequally; no externality, information gap, market power or public-good problem is identified. Policy A transfers $30 between participants without resource cost or changed behavior. Policy B makes the same transfer but destroys $8 of gains through changed allocation. Which assessment is correct?
options: Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.
Both policies correct a demonstrated efficiency failure because any unequal outcome is inefficient.
B must be more efficient because changing allocation proves it addresses a market failure.
A raises total surplus by $30 while B raises it by $22 because transfers are new resources.
q.commonError: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
q.feedback: An unequal split does not by itself demonstrate a missing efficiency condition. The costless transfer changes distribution; B additionally sacrifices $8 of gains. Whether that tradeoff is acceptable requires an equity judgment.

key: Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.

q.q: Atlas Coffee publishes verified wait times and prices. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Informational advertising
Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion

key: Informational advertising

q.q: Ivory Retail supports a tool that makes rival prices easy to compare. Which economic classification best fits?

q.q: Jasper Learning develops a genuinely improved tutoring format. Which economic classification best fits?

Strategic oligopoly collusion
Product innovation with possible temporary profit
q.feedback: An improved tutoring format changes the service itself. Buyers may value the improvement enough to support profit temporarily, while entry and imitation can erode it.

key: Product innovation with possible temporary profit

q.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=20, minimum-ATC output Q2=34.64, price $70.00 and MC=$50.00. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $50.00; excess capacity 20 units.
Markup $20.00; excess capacity 14.64 units.
Markup $20.00; excess capacity 34.64 units.
Markup $70.00; excess capacity 14.64 units.
q.feedback: Markup is P−MC=70.00−50.00=$20.00. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=34.64−20=14.64 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

q.q: Atlas Coffee publishes verified wait times and prices. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Atlas Coffee action?
options: Economic profit must become permanent
Search costs fall and demand responsiveness may change
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit
q.feedback: Publishing verified prices and wait times makes comparison less costly. It can alter demand and responsiveness, but does not establish a particular markup or permanent profit.

key: Search costs fall and demand responsiveness may change

q.q: Bloom Cosmetics links the brand to prestige without measurable performance claims. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Bloom Cosmetics action?

Economic profit must become permanent
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit

Price must equal marginal cost
ATC rises, but the initial MR=MC output is unchanged
All rival firms must exit
q.feedback: The order-independent sponsorship adds a fixed expense. Its cost effect raises ATC without changing MC; holding demand fixed isolates why the original MR=MC output is unchanged.

key: ATC rises, but the initial MR=MC output is unchanged

q.q: Ember Meals pays a platform fee on every order. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Ember Meals action?
options: Economic profit must become permanent
MC, AVC, and ATC rise, so output may fall
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit
q.feedback: A fee on each order adds to the cost of the marginal order and to average variable and total cost. With demand fixed, higher MC can reduce the profit-maximizing output.

key: MC, AVC, and ATC rise, so output may fall

q.q: Flint Apparel uses more durable fabric and better construction. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Flint Apparel action?
options: Demand may rise because delivered value increases, but resource cost must be counted
Economic profit must become permanent
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit
q.feedback: Better fabric and construction can raise willingness to pay, but the added materials and workmanship also use resources. A demand gain alone does not establish the net profit effect.

key: Demand may rise because delivered value increases, but resource cost must be counted

q.q: Glade Fitness creates switching benefits that make members less responsive to price. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Glade Fitness action?

q.q: Summit Coffee has demand P=118−2.2Q and MC=18+0.32Q. A new rival enters and lowers the demand intercept by $12. Demand slope and the entire cost function stay unchanged. Compared with the original profit-maximizing outcome, how do price and maximum economic profit change?
options: Price rises and profit falls: the lower quantity must raise the price along the original demand curve.
Price is unchanged and profit falls: unchanged MC fixes price at its original level.
Price falls and profit is unchanged: output adjustment fully offsets the demand reduction.
Both fall: weaker demand lowers the chosen price and the maximum profit obtainable from the unchanged cost curve.
q.feedback: The lower demand intercept reduces MR and the optimal output. With the stated linear demand and upward-sloping MC, price also falls. Revenue is lower at every positive output while costs are unchanged, so reoptimizing does not preserve the original maximum profit.

key: Both fall: weaker demand lowers the chosen price and the maximum profit obtainable from the unchanged cost curve.

q.q: Wren Foods faces demand P=120−2Q and marginal cost MC=18+0.3Q. Rival entry changes its demand to P=100−2Q, with costs unchanged. How does its profit-maximizing output change?
options: From 23.72 to 19.07 units.
From 19.07 to 23.72 units.
It stays at 23.72 units because the cost curve does not shift.
From 44.35 to 35.65 units.

q.q: Two rival cruise lines keep fares at $72 and sell 30 units each in the kinked-demand model shown. Rivals match fare cuts but do not match fare increases. A per-unit cost increase raises this firm’s constant MC from $48 to $54, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. How do its profit-maximizing fare, quantity and economic profit change?
options: Fare rises to $78 and quantity stays at 30; economic profit is unchanged.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit is unchanged because MR has a gap.
Fare falls and quantity rises; economic profit falls by less than $180.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit falls by $180.
q.feedback: At Q=30 the MR gap runs from $36 to $60. Both MC=$48 and MC=$54 fall inside it, so the optimum remains at the kink, P=$72 and Q=30. Cost rises $6 on each of 30 units, lowering profit by $180.
q.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
q.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

key: Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit falls by $180.

q.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown: P=70−0.5Q up to Q=20 and P=90−1.5Q above Q=20. Its constant MC initially equals $40. Compare a rise in MC to $45 with a rise to $55, holding demand fixed. Which conclusion is correct?
options: At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50.
At MC=$45 and MC=$55 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60 because any cost change lies inside the MR gap.
At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it expands output to Q=25 and lowers price to $52.50.
At MC=$45 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50; at MC=$55 it returns to Q=20 and P=$60.
q.feedback: At the kink MR drops from $50 to $30. MC=$45 lies within that range, but MC=$55 lies above it. On the upper demand branch MR=70−Q, so 70−Q=55 gives Q=15 and P=70−0.5×15=$62.50.
q.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 20, price 60, with two MR branches and MC at 40.
q.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=70−0.5Q for Q up to 20, then P=90−1.5Q for larger Q. At Q=20, the upper MR branch ends at 50 and the lower branch begins at 30. MC is horizontal at 40.

key: At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50.

q.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown, with prevailing price $72, quantity 30 and constant MC=$48. An input improvement lowers MC to $42, while a recurring license fee adds $300 to fixed cost. Demand does not change. Which evaluation correctly separates the output decision from the profit effect?
options: Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving exceeds the $300 fee, so economic profit rises by $120.
Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the $300 fee, so economic profit falls by $120.
The fixed fee raises MC above the MR gap, so quantity falls; the variable-cost saving cannot affect profit.
The lower MC moves quantity above the kink; the fixed fee is a variable cost, so profit is unchanged.
q.feedback: The MR gap at Q=30 is $36 to $60; MC=$42 remains inside it, so P and Q stay at $72 and 30. Variable cost falls by ($48−$42)×30=$180. The $300 fixed fee does not enter MC but exceeds that saving, reducing profit by $120.
q.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
q.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

key: Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the $300 fee, so economic profit falls by $120.

q.q: Use the displayed payoff matrix as the baseline. An enforceable agreement deducts 3 from the row firm’s payoff whenever it chooses B and 3 from the column firm’s payoff whenever it chooses Y, in every cell. Which comparison with the original game is correct?
options: The unique Nash outcome remains (B,Y) because an output-independent agreement cannot change any payoff.
Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are Nash outcomes after the deductions because the penalty leaves best responses unchanged.
The unique Nash outcome changes from (B,Y) to (A,X); (A,X) also remains the joint-payoff maximum.
The unique Nash outcome becomes (A,Y), because only the row firm changes its response.
q.feedback: Originally each firm prefers its noncooperative action. After deductions, row payoffs are A/X=10, A/Y=6, B/X=9, B/Y=5, so A is best against either column. Column payoffs analogously make X best against either row. Thus (A,X) is the unique equilibrium and gives the highest combined payoff, 20.

key: The unique Nash outcome changes from (B,Y) to (A,X); (A,X) also remains the joint-payoff maximum.

q.q: Use the displayed payoff matrix as the baseline. A coordination program adds 6 to each firm’s payoff only at (A,X), leaving all other cells unchanged. Which list contains all pure-strategy Nash equilibria after the change, and which outcome maximizes joint payoff?
options: Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are equilibria; (A,X) maximizes joint payoff at 32.
Only (A,X) is an equilibrium; improving that cell removes the incentive to choose B against Y.
Only (B,Y) is an equilibrium; the added payoff cannot alter any best response.
Both (A,Y) and (B,X) are equilibria; their unequal payoffs maximize the joint total.
q.feedback: The new (A,X) payoff is (16,16), so A is preferred to B against X and X to Y against A. Against Y, row still prefers B (7>5), and against B, column still prefers Y (7>5). Thus the old (B,Y) equilibrium also remains, while (A,X) yields the highest joint payoff.

key: Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are equilibria; (A,X) maximizes joint payoff at 32.

q.q: Market shares are 46%, 22%, 14%, 10% and 8%. The two smallest firms merge, with no other share changes. Which calculation and interpretation is correct?
options: CR4 stays 92% and HHI rises to 3120 because combining two small firms cannot change the top four.
CR4 rises to 100% and HHI stays 2960 because the combined market share is unchanged.
CR4 rises by 18 percentage points and HHI rises by 18 because the merging shares should be added to both indexes.
CR4 rises from 92% to 100% and HHI rises from 2960 to 3120; the measures describe concentration, not a complete prediction of conduct.
q.feedback: After merger the four shares are 46,22,18,14, so CR4=100%. The HHI increment is 2×10×8=160, making 3120. Conduct also depends on entry, substitution and behavior.

key: CR4 rises from 92% to 100% and HHI rises from 2960 to 3120; the measures describe concentration, not a complete prediction of conduct.

q.q: Market shares are 33%, 29%, 17%, 12% and 9%. Compare merger A (33% with 9%) with merger B (17% with 12%), holding other shares fixed. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both give CR4=100%, but A raises HHI by 594 and B by 408; equal CR4 does not imply the same HHI change.
Both give CR4=100% and the same HHI increase because each merger removes one firm.
A raises HHI less than B because one of its partners is the smallest firm.
CR4 stays 91% under both mergers because the original four largest shares are unchanged.
q.feedback: Each leaves four firms, so CR4 becomes 100%. HHI increments are 2×33×9=594 and 2×17×12=408. The product of the merging shares matters, not merely the smaller partner’s rank.

key: Both give CR4=100%, but A raises HHI by 594 and B by 408; equal CR4 does not imply the same HHI change.

q.q: Market shares are 40%, 26%, 15%, 11% and 8%. The 40% firm is split into two independent competitors, each with 20%, and all other shares stay fixed. Which comparison with the original concentration measures is correct?
options: CR4 remains 92% and HHI remains 2686 because the two new firms have the same combined share.
CR4 falls from 92% to 81%, and HHI falls from 2686 to 1886; the new shares must be reranked.
CR4 falls to 72% and HHI falls by only 20 because one new share should be omitted.
CR4 rises to 100% and HHI rises to 3486 because there are more competitors.
q.feedback: The new top four shares are 26,20,20,15, totaling 81. Replace 40² by 20²+20², reducing HHI by 800 to 1886. Independence, not merely a new label, is required for this calculation.

key: CR4 falls from 92% to 81%, and HHI falls from 2686 to 1886; the new shares must be reranked.

q.q: Market shares are 28%, 25%, 20%, 17% and 10%. Five percentage points move from the largest firm to the smallest, with all other shares fixed. Which updated concentration measures follow?
options: CR4=90% and HHI=2198 because the total share remains 100%.
CR4=95% and HHI=2328 because a growing small firm raises concentration.
CR4=85% and HHI=2068; rerank the new shares 25,23,20,17,15.
CR4=85% and HHI=2193 because HHI falls by exactly five points.
q.feedback: After the transfer shares are 23,25,20,17,15. The top four sum to 85. Squared shares sum to 529+625+400+289+225=2068.

key: CR4=85% and HHI=2068; rerank the new shares 25,23,20,17,15.

q.q: Market shares are 52%, 18%, 12%, 10% and 8%. The 18% and 12% firms propose merging. A report says the resulting HHI alone proves a precise price increase. Which response combines the calculation with its limitation?
options: HHI rises from 3336 to 3366, and the 30-point change is exactly the percentage price increase.
HHI stays 3336 because the merged firm’s combined share is unchanged, so no price effect is possible.
HHI rises to 3768, which by itself proves prices rise exactly 432%.
HHI rises from 3336 to 3768, but the price effect still requires evidence about substitution, entry, conduct and efficiencies.
q.feedback: The increment is 2×18×12=432, yielding 3768. HHI measures the distribution of market shares; it is not a formula converting concentration changes directly into price changes.

key: HHI rises from 3336 to 3768, but the price effect still requires evidence about substitution, entry, conduct and efficiencies.

q.q: Use the cartel graph with demand P=100−2Q and MC=$20. Two identical cartel members split the joint-profit-maximizing output equally. One secretly produces one additional unit while its rival holds its quota. Which comparison explains the incentive conflict?

q.q: A cartel member could earn an extra $12 million this year by secretly expanding output. If detected, it loses future profit with a present value of $30 million; detection probability is 60%. If undetected, future profit is unchanged. Under risk neutrality, which comparison determines whether to deviate?
options: The expected punishment is $18 million; comply because it exceeds the current gain.
The expected punishment is $30 million; comply because the full punishment is certain.
The expected punishment is $18 million; deviate because a current gain outweighs a larger discounted expected loss.
The expected punishment is $12 million; compare it with the $12 million gain using the probability of escaping detection.
q.feedback: The future loss is already a present value. Multiply it by detection probability: 0.6×$30 million=$18 million. Net expected gain from deviation is $-6 million, so compliance is preferred under the stated assumptions.

key: The expected punishment is $18 million; comply because it exceeds the current gain.

key: The deviator gains $45 while combined profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $45 deters this deviation.

q.q: Use the cartel graph with demand P=100−2Q and MC=$20. Compare a $200 lump-sum license charge on the cartel with a $10 tax per unit. The cartel stays active and reoptimizes jointly. Which comparison is correct?
options: The license leaves Q=20 and P=$60 with net profit $600; the per-unit tax gives Q=17.5 and P=$65 with net profit $612.50.

key: The license leaves Q=20 and P=$60 with net profit $600; the per-unit tax gives Q=17.5 and P=$65 with net profit $612.50.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Price lies below ATC but above AVC at the rising-MC output. What is the short-run decision?
options: Shut down and eliminate fixed cost
Produce at minimum ATC instead
Raise price to ATC
Produce and incur an economic loss
q.feedback: P above AVC means production covers variable cost and contributes toward unavoidable fixed cost. P below ATC means that contribution does not cover all fixed cost, so operating still incurs an economic loss.

The firm supplies zero in the short run and bears fixed cost
The firm breaks even

key: The firm supplies zero in the short run and bears fixed cost

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run benchmark, which two conditions hold?

P=MC and P=minimum ATC
P>MC and P>ATC
MC is below AVC

key: P=MC and P=minimum ATC

key: At the existing price the firm expands output and profit tends to rise; subsequent entry can increase market supply and lower price.
